about: Graph reader content (docs/anp-spec.md section 8.5, docs/anp-tools-contract.md). Every graph is drawn by tools/graphs.js from these numbers as SVG. x is shared by all panels; each panel has its own y axis (y.reverse: true draws it top-down, min at the top, as on a clinical audiogram). Series use visual-language classes and carry their label on the line (labelAt, in data units). regions are vertical bands a phase question can highlight (show: true draws one always). Question types: value (read a number: answer, tol, unit), phase (name a phase or region: options, correct, highlight) and shift (predict the change: options, correct, overlay drawn after answering). Item ids graphs:<graph>:<question> are permanent. A question may carry its own topic (never earlier than the graph's). Validator: scripts/lib/anp-tool-checks/graphs.mjs. The numbers are schematic but physiologically typical for a resting adult.

graphs.title: The pH scale is logarithmic
graphs.intro: Blood pH looks like it barely moves, from 7.35 to 7.45. This graph shows what those small numbers mean for the hydrogen ion concentration.
graphs.alt: Hydrogen ion concentration in nanomoles per liter plotted against pH from 6.8 to 7.8. The curve falls steeply: about 158 at pH 6.8, 100 at 7.0, 40 at 7.4 and 16 at 7.8. A shaded band marks the normal blood pH range, 7.35 to 7.45.

questions.q: Read the hydrogen ion concentration at pH 7.4, the middle of the normal range.
questions.why: Go up from pH 7.4 to the curve, then across: about 40 nmol/L, that is 0.00000004 mol/L. That tiny concentration is the normal hydrogen ion level of your blood.

questions.q: At what pH has the hydrogen ion concentration doubled, from 40 to 80 nmol/L?
questions.why: Go across from 80 nmol/L to the curve, then down: pH 7.1. A fall of only 0.3 pH units doubles the hydrogen ion concentration, because pH is logarithmic: every 0.3 units is a factor of 2, and every 1 unit is a factor of 10.

questions.q: A blood sample has a pH of 7.28. Which region of the graph is it in?
options: Acidosis
The normal range
Alkalosis

why.correct: 7.28 is below 7.35, so the blood is too acidic: acidosis. Its hydrogen ion concentration, about 52 nmol/L, is 30 percent above normal.
options: Right: any blood pH below 7.35 is acidosis.
The normal range is 7.35 to 7.45, the narrow shaded band. 7.28 is below it.
Alkalosis means a pH above 7.45, with fewer hydrogen ions than normal. 7.28 is on the acid side.

questions.q: A patient's blood pH falls from 7.4 to 7.1. How does the hydrogen ion concentration change?
options: It doubles, from about 40 to about 80 nmol/L
It rises by about 4 percent, because 7.1 is about 4 percent less than 7.4
It falls, because the pH number fell
It rises tenfold

why.correct: Moving 0.3 units left along the curve doubles the hydrogen ion concentration. That is why a pH of 7.1 is a medical emergency even though the number changed so little.
options: Right: each 0.3 fall in pH doubles the hydrogen ion concentration.
pH is a logarithm, not an ordinary number. A 0.3 fall is not a 4 percent change; it is a doubling.
pH and hydrogen ion concentration move in opposite directions: a lower pH means more hydrogen ions.
A tenfold rise takes a fall of a whole pH unit, from 7.4 to 6.4. A 0.3 fall doubles it.

graphs.title: Flow vs radius: the fourth-power curve
graphs.intro: Flow through a tube depends on the fourth power of its radius. Keep the pressure gradient fixed and change only the radius.
graphs.alt: Flow as a percentage of starting flow plotted against radius as a percentage of starting radius. The curve is flat at small radii and rises ever more steeply: 6 percent flow at half radius, 41 percent at 80 percent radius, 100 at 100 and 244 at 125. A straight dashed line shows what flow would be if it were simply proportional to radius.

questions.q: A vessel narrows to 80% of its starting radius. Read the new flow, as a percentage of the starting flow.
questions.why: About 41%. 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.8 = 0.41, so narrowing the radius by one fifth cuts flow by more than half.

questions.q: Read the flow when the radius is halved, to 50%.
questions.why: About 6%, one sixteenth of the start: ½ × ½ × ½ × ½ = 1/16. Halving the radius raises resistance 16-fold, and flow falls to match.

questions.q: In which range of radius does a 25-point change in radius change flow the most?
options: Between 100% and 125%
Between 0% and 25%
Between 25% and 50%

why.correct: The curve is steepest where the radius is largest: from 100% to 125% radius, flow rises from 100% to about 244%.
options: Right: the fourth-power curve keeps getting steeper, so the same change in radius does most at large radii.
Here the curve is almost flat: flow only rises from 0 to about 0.4%.
Flow rises only from about 0.4% to 6% here. The curve steepens as radius grows.

questions.q: The pressure gradient across the vessel doubles, and nothing else changes. How does the curve change?
options: Every point doubles: twice the flow at each radius
The curve shifts right: you need a wider radius for the same flow
No change: flow depends only on radius
Flow halves at every radius

why.correct: Flow equals pressure gradient divided by resistance. Resistance at each radius is unchanged, so doubling the gradient doubles the flow at every radius. The curve rises twice as steeply and reaches 200% flow at the starting radius.
options: Right: F = ΔP/R, and R is the same at each radius, so every flow doubles.
Shifting the curve right would mean less flow at each radius. A bigger gradient pushes more flow through the same tube.
Flow depends on both the gradient and the resistance. The radius sets the resistance; the gradient is the push.
Halving would follow a smaller gradient, or doubled resistance. A doubled gradient doubles flow.

graphs.title: Enzyme activity vs temperature
graphs.intro: A typical human enzyme, tested across a range of temperatures. Activity is shown as a percentage of the fastest rate.
graphs.alt: Enzyme activity as a percentage of maximum plotted against temperature from 0 to 70 degrees Celsius. Activity rises gradually from about 6 percent at 0 degrees to a peak of 100 percent near 37 degrees, then falls steeply to near zero by 60 degrees.

questions.q: Read the temperature at which this enzyme is most active.
questions.why: The peak is near 37 °C, close to your body temperature. Human enzymes work best near the temperature your body holds them at.

questions.q: Read the enzyme's activity at 20 °C.
questions.why: About 30% of maximum. In the cold, molecules move more slowly, so substrate and enzyme collide less often and fewer collisions have enough energy. The enzyme itself is not damaged.

questions.q: In which region does activity fall because the enzyme's shape is being destroyed?
options: Above about 40 °C
Below about 20 °C
Between 30 and 37 °C

why.correct: Above the optimum, heat breaks the weak bonds that hold the enzyme in shape. The active site loses its shape: the enzyme is denatured.
options: Right: the steep fall above about 40 °C is denaturation.
Activity is low in the cold because molecules move slowly, not because the enzyme's shape is lost. Warm it up and it works again.
Activity is rising here as collisions get faster. Nothing is being destroyed yet.

questions.q: A sample of the enzyme is held at 60 °C for an hour, then cooled and tested again at every temperature. How does the curve change?
options: It flattens near zero at every temperature
It is unchanged: once cooled, the enzyme works as before
Its peak moves to 60 °C, because the enzyme has adapted
It rises everywhere, because heating activates the enzyme

why.correct: Heat denaturation is usually permanent: the unfolded chains tangle and stick together and cannot refold, so the damage does not reverse on cooling. Cooling slows a healthy enzyme; it does not repair a denatured one.
options: Right: the enzyme's shape is lost for good, so it stays inactive at every temperature.
Cooling does not restore a denatured shape. Only the slowing caused by cold is reversible.
Enzyme molecules do not adapt. The peak stays where it was; the damaged molecules simply stop working.
Heat past the optimum destroys the active site; it never makes the enzyme better.

graphs.title: Enzyme activity vs pH
graphs.intro: Two human enzymes tested across a range of pH: one that works in the stomach and one that works in the blood.
graphs.alt: Enzyme activity as a percentage of maximum plotted against pH from 0 to 10. A stomach enzyme peaks at pH 2 and falls to near zero by pH 5. An enzyme working in the blood peaks at pH 7.4 and falls off on either side, to near zero below pH 5.5 and above pH 9.3.

questions.q: Read the optimum pH of the stomach enzyme.
questions.why: Its peak is at about pH 2, matching the strongly acidic fluid it works in.

questions.q: Over what range of pH does the stomach enzyme work at more than half its maximum?
options: About pH 1 to 3.5
About pH 6.5 to 8.3
About pH 0 to 10
About pH 4 to 6

why.correct: Its curve is above 50% only between about pH 1 and 3.5. Outside that range the charges on its active site change and substrate binds poorly.
options: Right: read where the stomach enzyme's curve is above 50 on the vertical axis.
That is the range for the enzyme in the blood, whose peak is at 7.4.
Each enzyme works only in a narrow band of pH; no enzyme works well across the whole scale.
The stomach enzyme is almost inactive here, below 25% and falling.

questions.q: A person's blood pH falls from 7.4 to 7.0 (acidosis). How does the blood enzyme's activity change?
options: It falls a little, to about 90% of maximum
It stops completely
It rises, because enzymes work faster in acid
It does not change

why.correct: Moving left from the optimum takes activity down the curve, to about 90%. The same shift happens to many enzymes at once, and bigger shifts cut activity further, which is part of why acidosis disrupts so many body processes.
options: Right: pH 7.0 is on the left slope of the curve, a little below the peak.
Activity only falls to zero far from the optimum, below about pH 5.5.
Each enzyme has its own optimum. This one works best at 7.4; more acid moves it away from that.
pH changes the charges on the enzyme's active site, so moving off the optimum changes activity.

graphs.title: A regulated variable around its set point
graphs.intro: Your body temperature over an hour. At 10 minutes you step out into the cold. Watch negative feedback pull the temperature back.
graphs.alt: Body temperature from 36 to 39 degrees Celsius over 60 minutes. It holds near the 37 degree set point, dips to 36.6 degrees after cold exposure at 10 minutes, overshoots to 37.2 at about 24 minutes, and settles back to 37 with smaller swings, staying inside the normal range band from 36.5 to 37.5.

questions.q: Read the lowest temperature reached after you step into the cold.
questions.why: About 36.6 °C, at around 16 minutes. The loop takes time to detect the fall and get its effectors working, so the temperature keeps falling for a few minutes first.

questions.q: Read the set point the temperature swings around.
questions.why: 37 °C, the dashed line. The set point is the target the control center compares the sensed temperature with.

questions.q: Between about 21 and 28 minutes, the temperature is above the set point. What is the loop doing then?
options: Lowering the temperature: the response now opposes a rise
Raising the temperature further: this is positive feedback
Nothing: the loop only acts when the temperature is below the set point

why.correct: The warming response overshot, so the loop reverses: warm blood is sent to the skin, heat loss rises, and the temperature comes back down. Negative feedback opposes a change in either direction.
options: Right: negative feedback opposes any move away from the set point, up or down.
Positive feedback would push the temperature further up and further away. Instead it turns back toward 37 °C.
The loop corrects both falls and rises; it is the same loop working in the opposite direction.

questions.q: At 30 minutes, an infection makes the control center raise the set point to 38.5 °C. How does the graph change after that?
options: The temperature climbs, then swings around 38.5 °C
The loop stops working, so the temperature drifts without control
The temperature keeps rising without limit: positive feedback
The temperature stays at 37 °C, because the loop resists any change

why.correct: The loop still works; only its target has moved. Now 37 °C reads as too cold, so the body conserves and makes heat until the temperature reaches the new set point. The same negative feedback then holds it there, swinging around 38.5 °C.
options: Right: the same negative feedback now defends 38.5 °C.
The loop keeps regulating, just around the new target: the temperature settles instead of drifting.
It stops rising at the new set point. Positive feedback would have no stopping point inside the loop.
The loop compares with its set point. Once that is 38.5 °C, a temperature of 37 °C is an error to correct.

graphs.title: The resting potential and the equilibrium potentials
graphs.intro: A neuron's membrane potential over 10 minutes, with the equilibrium potentials of potassium and sodium drawn in. At 4 minutes the potassium outside the cell starts to rise.
graphs.alt: Membrane potential from minus 100 to plus 80 millivolts over 10 minutes. The resting potential sits at minus 70, much closer to the potassium equilibrium potential at minus 90 than to the sodium equilibrium potential at plus 60.

questions.q: Read the resting membrane potential.
questions.why: About −70 mV: the inside of the membrane is 70 millivolts negative compared with the outside.

questions.q: Read potassium's equilibrium potential: the voltage at which potassium's electrical pull exactly balances its concentration gradient.
questions.why: About −90 mV. At that voltage the negative inside pulls potassium in exactly as hard as its concentration gradient pushes it out, so there is no net flow.

questions.q: The resting potential sits much closer to one equilibrium potential than the other. Which, and why?
options: Potassium's, because at rest the membrane is far more permeable to potassium
Sodium's, because there is more sodium outside the cell
Halfway between them, because the pump moves both ions
Potassium's, because the pump moves more potassium than sodium

why.correct: The membrane potential is pulled toward the equilibrium potential of whichever ion can cross most easily. At rest many potassium leak channels are open and few sodium channels are, so the voltage sits near potassium's −90 mV, nudged up to −70 by the small sodium leak.
options: Right: permeability decides which ion's equilibrium potential the membrane approaches.
Sodium is far from equilibrium at rest, but few channels let it in, so it has only a small effect.
−70 mV is 20 mV from potassium's value and 130 mV from sodium's: nowhere near halfway.
The pump moves 3 sodium out for 2 potassium in, and its direct electrical effect is only a few millivolts. Permeability, not the pump, sets where the voltage sits.

questions.q: From 4 minutes, blood potassium rises (hyperkalemia), so the potassium concentration outside the cell rises. How does the graph change?
options: The potassium and resting lines rise toward zero
The resting potential hyperpolarizes, moving further from zero
Only sodium's equilibrium potential changes
Nothing changes: the pump restores the gradient at once

why.correct: More potassium outside means a smaller concentration gradient pushing potassium out, so less negative charge is needed to balance it: the equilibrium potential rises toward zero. The resting potential follows it up and the cell is depolarized. That is why high blood potassium can disturb the heartbeat.
options: Right: a smaller potassium gradient moves both lines up.
Less potassium leaves when there is more outside, so the inside becomes less negative, not more.
Sodium's equilibrium potential depends on the sodium gradient, which has not changed.
The pump cannot remove potassium from the blood around the cell; the outside concentration stays high while blood potassium is high.

graphs.title: A neuron action potential
graphs.intro: The voltage across a patch of neuron membrane. A weak stimulus arrives at about 0.5 ms, and a stronger one at about 2.5 ms.
graphs.alt: Membrane potential in millivolts over 8 milliseconds. A small bump from minus 70 to about minus 61 fades away. A second depolarization reaches threshold at minus 55 and becomes an action potential that peaks near plus 30 millivolts, falls back past minus 70 to about minus 80, and returns to minus 70 by about 7 milliseconds.

questions.q: Read the peak voltage of the action potential.
questions.why: About +30 mV: at the peak the inside of the membrane is positive, because so much sodium has rushed in.

questions.q: Read the threshold voltage, where the second depolarization takes off.
questions.why: About −55 mV. At threshold, enough voltage-gated sodium channels open that sodium entry outpaces potassium exit, and the depolarization feeds on itself.

questions.q: Name the phase in which the voltage dips below −70 mV because potassium channels are slow to close.
options: Hyperpolarization
Depolarization
Repolarization
Graded potential

why.correct: Extra potassium leaves while the slow voltage-gated potassium channels close, carrying the voltage below rest toward potassium's equilibrium potential.
options: Right: below the resting potential is hyperpolarization.
Depolarization is the rise toward and above zero, driven by sodium entry.
Repolarization is the fall from the peak back toward rest. The dip below rest comes after it.
The graded potential is the small early bump that never reached threshold.

questions.q: Why did the first bump, near 1 ms, not become an action potential?
options: It was a graded potential that never reached threshold
The membrane was in its refractory period
It was an action potential, just a small one
Sodium channels opened, but potassium channels canceled them out

why.correct: The weak stimulus made a small graded depolarization, to about −61 mV. It never reached −55 mV, so the voltage-gated sodium channels never opened in large numbers, and the bump faded away.
options: Right: below threshold, a graded potential just fades.
No action potential had happened yet, so the membrane was not refractory.
Action potentials are all-or-none: there is no small version. Anything smaller than full size is a graded potential.
Voltage-gated sodium channels open in large numbers only at threshold, which this bump never reached.

questions.q: The second stimulus is made twice as strong. How does the action potential change?
options: It reaches threshold sooner, with the same peak
It peaks twice as high, near +60 mV
It lasts twice as long
It is smaller, because the channels are overloaded

why.correct: A stronger stimulus makes a bigger graded potential, so threshold is reached a little sooner. But action potentials are all-or-none: once the sodium channels open, the action potential runs its fixed course and peaks at the same voltage. Nerve cells signal a stronger stimulus by firing more action potentials each second, not bigger ones.
options: Right: same size, a little earlier.
The peak is set by the sodium gradient and the channels, not by the stimulus. It stays near +30 mV.
The duration is set by how the sodium and potassium channels open and close, which does not depend on stimulus strength.
Once threshold is reached, the full action potential happens every time.

graphs.title: Ventricular muscle action potential
graphs.intro: One action potential in a contractile cell of the left ventricle. Compare its shape and length with the neuron's.
graphs.alt: Membrane potential in millivolts over 400 milliseconds. From rest at minus 90, a rapid upstroke to about plus 20 (phase 0) is followed by a small notch (phase 1), a long plateau near 0 millivolts lasting about 200 milliseconds (phase 2), repolarization back to minus 90 by about 290 milliseconds (phase 3), and rest (phase 4).

questions.q: Read the resting membrane potential of this contractile cell.
questions.why: About −90 mV, more negative than a neuron's −70 mV. Contractile cells have very few open sodium channels at rest, so their voltage sits almost at potassium's equilibrium potential.

questions.q: Read how long the action potential lasts, from the upstroke to full repolarization.
questions.why: About 250 to 300 ms, from the upstroke at about 20 ms to rest again near 290 ms. A neuron's action potential lasts about 2 ms: more than a hundred times shorter.

questions.q: Which phase depends on calcium entering through L-type calcium channels?
options: The plateau (phase 2)
The rapid upstroke (phase 0)
Repolarization (phase 3)
Rest (phase 4)

why.correct: During the plateau, calcium entering through L-type channels balances potassium leaving, so the voltage stays near 0 mV for about 200 ms. That calcium also triggers contraction.
options: Right: calcium in, potassium out, voltage held steady.
The upstroke is driven by sodium rushing in through fast voltage-gated sodium channels.
Repolarization happens when the calcium channels close and potassium exit wins.
At rest, potassium leak channels set the voltage; the L-type channels are closed.

questions.q: Why can't a rapid series of stimuli make heart muscle stay contracted, as skeletal muscle does in tetanus?
options: Its refractory period lasts almost as long as the contraction
It has no voltage-gated sodium channels
Its calcium is never removed from the cytosol
Its resting potential is too negative to reach threshold

why.correct: The cell cannot fire again until it has nearly repolarized, about 250 ms after the upstroke, by which time the contraction is ending. So each contraction relaxes before the next begins, and the heart can always refill between beats.
options: Right: the long plateau makes the refractory period long.
The rapid upstroke is made by voltage-gated sodium channels, so the cell has them.
Calcium is pumped back out of the cytosol at the end of every beat, which is why the cell relaxes.
Current from neighboring cells brings it to threshold every beat.

questions.q: A drug partly blocks L-type calcium channels. How does the action potential change, and what happens to contraction?
options: The plateau shortens and contraction weakens
The upstroke disappears, so the cell cannot fire
The plateau lengthens and contraction strengthens
Nothing changes, because the action potential does not depend on calcium

why.correct: With less calcium entering, potassium exit wins sooner, so the plateau sags and ends early. Less calcium also means less calcium-induced calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so each contraction is weaker. Drugs that block these channels are used to lower blood pressure and heart workload.
options: Right: shorter plateau, less trigger calcium, weaker contraction.
The upstroke is carried by sodium channels, which the drug does not block.
Blocking calcium entry removes the current that holds the plateau up, so it shortens.
The plateau is held up by calcium entry, so blocking it changes the shape.

graphs.title: Pacemaker potential of the SA node
graphs.intro: The voltage of an SA node pacemaker cell over three heartbeats. Unlike a contractile cell, it has no stable resting potential.
graphs.alt: Membrane potential of an SA node cell over 2.4 seconds. After each action potential, the voltage falls to about minus 60 millivolts, then drifts slowly upward to the threshold at minus 40, fires an action potential peaking near plus 10, and repeats every 0.8 seconds.

questions.q: Read the time from one action potential peak to the next.
questions.why: 0.8 s. One beat every 0.8 s is 60 ÷ 0.8 = 75 beats per minute, a normal resting heart rate.

questions.q: Read the most negative voltage these cells reach.
questions.why: About −60 mV, less negative than a contractile cell's −90. The cell never settles there: it starts drifting upward at once.

questions.q: What is the slow upward drift between action potentials called?
options: The pacemaker potential
The plateau
Repolarization
Hyperpolarization

why.correct: The pacemaker potential is a spontaneous depolarization: channels that open as the cell repolarizes let positive ions leak in (the funny current), then calcium channels add more near threshold. It brings the cell to threshold with no outside trigger.
options: Right: the slow drift to threshold is the pacemaker potential.
The plateau belongs to the contractile cell's action potential; pacemaker cells have none.
Repolarization is the fall after each peak. The drift rises.
Hyperpolarization would move the voltage down, away from threshold.

questions.q: Sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine onto the SA node. How does the graph change?
options: The drift steepens and beats come closer together
The pacemaker potential flattens, so beats come further apart
The peaks get taller, but the timing stays the same
The threshold moves up to 0 mV

why.correct: Norepinephrine opens more of the channels behind the drift, so positive ions leak in faster, the pacemaker potential rises more steeply and threshold arrives sooner. Here each beat takes 0.55 s: about 109 beats per minute.
options: Right: steeper drift, shorter time to threshold, faster heart rate.
A flatter drift is what acetylcholine from the vagus nerves does.
Heart rate is set by how fast the cell reaches threshold, not by how tall the peaks are.
Threshold is set by the voltage-gated channels and stays near −40 mV.

questions.q: The vagus nerves release acetylcholine onto the SA node. How does the graph change?
options: The drift flattens and beats come further apart
The drift gets steeper, so beats come closer together
The cells stop firing completely
The peaks get taller

why.correct: Acetylcholine opens extra potassium channels, which pull the starting voltage lower, and slows the inward leak, which flattens the drift. Threshold comes later: here one beat each 1.1 s, about 55 per minute.
options: Right: lower start, flatter drift, slower heart rate.
A steeper drift is the sympathetic effect.
Normal vagal activity slows the SA node but does not stop it; at rest it holds the rate below the node's own intrinsic rate.
The timing, not the height, changes.

graphs.title: ECG waves and intervals
graphs.intro: Two normal beats recorded from one lead, on standard ECG paper: each small square is 0.04 s wide and 0.1 mV tall.
graphs.alt: Two normal ECG beats over 1.6 seconds on grid paper. Each beat has a small rounded P wave, a flat PR segment, a tall narrow QRS complex peaking at 1.2 millivolts, a flat ST segment and a rounded T wave. R waves are 0.8 seconds apart.

questions.q: Read the PR interval of the first beat, from the start of the P wave to the start of the QRS complex. Each small square is 0.04 s.
questions.why: The P wave starts at 0.04 s and the QRS complex at 0.20 s: 0.16 s, four small squares. A normal PR interval is 0.12 to 0.20 s. Most of it is the AV nodal delay.

questions.q: Read the time from one R wave to the next, then work out the heart rate in beats per minute.
questions.why: The R waves are at 0.24 s and 1.04 s, 0.8 s apart. 60 s ÷ 0.8 s per beat = 75 beats per minute.

questions.q: Which part of the trace shows the ventricles depolarizing?
options: The QRS complex
The P wave
The T wave
The ST segment

why.correct: The QRS complex is large because the ventricles hold the most muscle, and narrow because Purkinje fibers spread the impulse through them in under 0.1 s.
options: Right: QRS is ventricular depolarization.
The P wave is atrial depolarization, which is why it is small.
The T wave is ventricular repolarization.
During the ST segment the whole ventricle is depolarized, in its plateau, so the trace is flat.

questions.q: The atria repolarize too, but no wave for it appears. Where is it?
options: Inside the QRS complex
It is the T wave
The atria never repolarize
It is the P wave

why.correct: Atrial repolarization happens while the ventricles depolarize. Its small signal is swamped by the much larger QRS complex.
options: Right: it coincides with, and is hidden by, the QRS complex.
The T wave is ventricular repolarization.
Every cell that fires must repolarize before it can fire again, atrial cells included.
The P wave is atrial depolarization; repolarization comes later.

questions.q: Conduction through the AV node slows (first-degree heart block). How does the trace change?
options: The PR interval lengthens
The QRS complex widens
The P waves disappear
The T waves turn upside down

why.correct: The PR interval is mostly AV nodal delay, so slower AV conduction lengthens it, here to 0.28 s. Once through the node the impulse spreads normally, so the QRS complex keeps its shape and every P wave is still followed by a QRS complex.
options: Right: a longer PR interval is the only change.
A wide QRS means slow spread through the ventricles, below the AV node.
The atria still depolarize normally; the delay comes after them.
Repolarization of the ventricles is not affected by a delay above them.

graphs.title: The cardiac cycle (Wiggers diagram)
graphs.intro: One heartbeat of the left heart at 75 beats per minute, 0.8 s. Pressures, ventricular volume, the ECG and the heart sounds share one time axis, so you can read down to see what happens at the same moment.
graphs.alt: Four stacked panels over 0.8 seconds. Top: aortic pressure between 80 and 120 millimeters of mercury, left ventricular pressure rising from near 5 to 121 and back, and left atrial pressure between 4 and 12. Second: left ventricular volume from 130 milliliters down to 60 and back. Third: the ECG with P, QRS and T. Bottom: the first heart sound at 0.20 to 0.26 seconds and the second at 0.52 to 0.56 seconds. Dashed lines mark the mitral valve closing at 0.205 seconds, the aortic valve opening at 0.25, the aortic valve closing at 0.52 and the mitral valve opening at 0.60.

questions.q: Read the end-diastolic volume, the most blood the ventricle holds.
questions.why: About 130 mL, reached just as the mitral valve closes at the start of systole.

questions.q: Work out the stroke volume: end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume.
questions.why: 130 mL minus the lowest volume, about 60 mL: 70 mL ejected. That is an ejection fraction of 70 ÷ 130, about 54%.

questions.q: Read the aortic pressure at the moment the aortic valve opens, the lowest aortic pressure in the cycle.
questions.why: About 80 mm Hg. The ventricle must raise its pressure above this before the aortic valve opens; that is what isovolumetric contraction does.

questions.q: Between about 0.20 and 0.25 s, pressure in the ventricle climbs steeply but its volume does not change. Name this phase.
options: Isovolumetric contraction
Ventricular ejection
Isovolumetric relaxation
Atrial systole

why.correct: Both valves are shut: ventricular pressure is above atrial pressure (mitral closed) but still below aortic pressure (aortic closed). The muscle contracts on a fixed volume of blood.
options: Right: iso- means same, volumetric means volume.
Ejection begins only when the aortic valve opens, at about 0.25 s, and then volume falls.
Isovolumetric relaxation is the other flat-volume phase, after ejection, when pressure falls.
Atrial systole comes before this, while the mitral valve is still open and volume is still rising.

questions.q: What makes the second heart sound, at about 0.52 s?
options: The aortic and pulmonary valves closing
The ventricular muscle contracting
The mitral and tricuspid valves closing
Blood rushing into the relaxed ventricles

why.correct: As the ventricles relax, their pressure drops below aortic pressure. Blood starts to flow back, fills the valve cusps and snaps them shut; the vibration is the sound. The little notch on the aortic pressure line marks the same moment.
options: Right: S2 is the semilunar valves closing.
Heart sounds come from valves closing, not from the muscle.
The AV valves close at the start of systole: that is the first heart sound.
Rapid filling begins later, when the mitral valve opens at about 0.60 s.

questions.q: At about 0.60 s, left ventricular pressure falls below left atrial pressure. What happens?
options: The mitral valve opens
The aortic valve closes
The mitral valve closes
The aortic valve opens

why.correct: The mitral valve opens whenever the atrium's pressure is higher than the ventricle's. Blood that has been collecting in the atrium rushes in, and the volume line climbs steeply.
options: Right: the pressure gradient now points from atrium to ventricle.
The aortic valve closed earlier, at about 0.52 s, when ventricular pressure fell below aortic pressure.
The mitral valve closes when ventricular pressure rises above atrial pressure, at the start of systole.
The aortic valve opens only when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure, around 80 mm Hg.

questions.q: Heart rate rises to 150 beats per minute, so each cycle lasts 0.4 s instead of 0.8 s. How does the volume curve change, and which part of the cycle is cut most?
options: Diastole shrinks most, and end-diastolic volume falls a little
Ejection shrinks most, while the time for filling stays the same
Every phase shrinks by exactly half
Nothing changes except that the ECG waves come closer together

why.correct: Systole shortens only a little as the rate rises; most of the time saved comes out of diastole. The flat, slow late-filling period almost disappears first, which costs little, so end-diastolic volume falls only a little. At very high rates the time for filling becomes too short and stroke volume falls.
options: Right: diastole takes the cut.
Ejection shortens somewhat, but much less than diastole.
The phases do not shrink evenly: systole is far less compressible than diastole.
The mechanical cycle changes along with the electrical one; the time for filling shrinks.

graphs.title: Pressure–volume loop
graphs.intro: The same heartbeat as the Wiggers diagram, drawn as left ventricular pressure against volume. Time runs counterclockwise around the loop.
graphs.alt: A counterclockwise loop of left ventricular pressure against volume. The bottom edge is filling, from 60 to 130 milliliters at low pressure. The right edge rises straight up at 130 milliliters from 10 to 81 millimeters of mercury. The top curve is ejection, from 130 down to 60 milliliters, peaking near 121. The left edge falls straight down at 60 milliliters from 94 to 9.

questions.q: Read the stroke volume from the width of the loop.
questions.why: The loop runs from 130 mL (end-diastolic volume) to 60 mL (end-systolic volume): 70 mL ejected each beat.

questions.q: Read the ventricular pressure at which the aortic valve opens.
questions.why: About 80 mm Hg, the top of the right edge. The valve opens when ventricular pressure just exceeds the pressure in the aorta.

questions.q: Which part of the loop is isovolumetric relaxation?
options: The vertical line at about 60 mL, where pressure falls
The vertical line at about 130 mL, where pressure rises
The curved top
The nearly flat bottom

why.correct: After the aortic valve closes, the ventricle relaxes with both valves shut, so pressure falls at a fixed volume, the end-systolic volume.
options: Right: pressure falls while volume stays at about 60 mL.
That rising vertical line is isovolumetric contraction.
The curved top is ejection: volume falls as blood leaves.
The bottom is filling: volume rises at low pressure.

questions.q: More blood returns to the heart, so preload rises, while contractility and afterload stay the same. How does the loop change?
options: It widens to the right: end-diastolic volume and stroke volume both rise
It gets taller: the aortic valve opens at a higher pressure
It narrows from the left: end-systolic volume rises
It does not change

why.correct: More filling moves the bottom-right corner to a larger volume. By the Frank–Starling mechanism the stretched muscle contracts harder and ejects to about the same end-systolic volume, so the loop is wider: here stroke volume rises from 70 to about 84 mL.
options: Right: a wider loop means a bigger stroke volume.
A taller loop is what a higher afterload does.
A higher end-systolic volume follows a higher afterload or weaker contraction, not more filling.
Preload sets end-diastolic volume, which is one side of the loop.

questions.q: Aortic pressure is higher, so afterload rises, while preload and contractility stay the same. How does the loop change?
options: It gets taller and narrower
It widens: stroke volume rises
It moves left as a whole, keeping its width
It does not change

why.correct: The ventricle must build more pressure before the aortic valve opens, so the valve opens later, at a higher pressure. With the same contractility it cannot squeeze as far, so ejection stops at a larger end-systolic volume. Here stroke volume falls from 70 to about 56 mL.
options: Right: taller and narrower.
More resistance to ejection means less blood ejected, not more.
End-diastolic volume, the right side, has not changed; only end-systolic volume moves.
Afterload is the pressure the ventricle ejects against, so the ejection phase changes.

graphs.title: The Frank–Starling curve
graphs.intro: How the stroke volume of a healthy left ventricle depends on how full it is before it contracts, with contractility held constant.
graphs.alt: Stroke volume in milliliters plotted against left ventricular end-diastolic volume. The curve rises steeply from about 10 milliliters at 40 milliliters of filling, passes 70 at 130, and levels off near 95 above 200. A marked point shows rest at 130 and 70.

questions.q: Read the stroke volume at an end-diastolic volume of 130 mL.
questions.why: About 70 mL, a typical resting stroke volume.

questions.q: Venous return rises, and end-diastolic volume goes from 130 to 175 mL. Read the new stroke volume.
questions.why: About 86 mL. More stretch gave a stronger contraction, with no change in contractility: that is the Frank–Starling mechanism.

questions.q: Over which range does extra filling add the least stroke volume?
options: Above about 200 mL
Between 60 and 120 mL
Below 60 mL

why.correct: The curve flattens at high volumes: the muscle fibers are near their best length, and the stiff pericardium limits further stretch, so more filling adds little.
options: Right: the flat part of the curve.
This is the steep part: each extra milliliter of filling adds the most stroke volume here.
The curve is rising here too; filling still adds stroke volume.

questions.q: Sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine onto the ventricles. How does the curve shift?
options: Up: more stroke volume at every end-diastolic volume
Along the same curve to the right
Down: less stroke volume at every end-diastolic volume
No change: only filling sets stroke volume

why.correct: Norepinephrine raises contractility: more calcium enters each cell and more is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, so the muscle contracts harder at any stretch. A change in contractility moves you to a new curve; a change in filling moves you along the same one.
options: Right: higher contractility lifts the whole curve.
Moving along the curve is what a change in filling does. Norepinephrine changes the curve itself.
Lower contractility lowers the curve; norepinephrine raises it.
Filling moves you along a curve, but contractility decides which curve you are on.

questions.q: A heart attack scars part of the left ventricle, and its contractility falls. How does the curve shift?
options: It shifts down and flattens
Up, because the remaining muscle is stretched more
No change: the curve depends only on filling
Left, so the same stroke volume needs less filling

why.correct: Scar tissue does not contract, so the ventricle generates less force at every stretch: less stroke volume at every end-diastolic volume, and extra filling helps less. To eject even a modest stroke volume it must fill to a much larger volume, which raises the pressure in the atrium and in the veins behind it.
options: Right: a lower, flatter curve.
Stretch cannot make up for lost muscle; the whole curve drops.
Contractility sets which curve the heart is on; losing muscle lowers it.
Shifting the curve left would mean a stronger heart. Losing muscle does the opposite.

graphs.title: Pressure along the vascular tree
graphs.intro: Blood pressure at each level of the systemic circuit, from the aorta back to the venae cavae, in a person at rest lying down.
graphs.alt: Blood pressure from the aorta to the venae cavae. In the aorta and large arteries the pressure swings between 80 and 120 millimeters of mercury with each beat, around a mean of about 93. Across the arterioles it falls steeply to about 35 and the swings die out. It falls to about 15 across the capillaries, then slowly to near 2 in the venae cavae.

questions.q: Read the pressure as blood enters the capillaries.
questions.why: About 35 mm Hg. More than half of the mean arterial pressure has already been used up pushing blood through the arterioles.

questions.q: Read the mean arterial pressure in the aorta.
questions.why: About 93 mm Hg. It sits closer to the diastolic 80 than the systolic 120 because diastole lasts longer: 80 + (120 − 80) ÷ 3 ≈ 93.

questions.q: Where along the circuit does pressure fall most steeply?
options: Across the arterioles
Across the capillaries
Along the aorta and large arteries
Along the veins

why.correct: Pressure falls most where resistance is greatest. Arterioles are narrow and wrapped in smooth muscle, so they are the main resistance vessels, and they also damp out the beat-to-beat swings.
options: Right: the arterioles are where most of the pressure is spent.
Capillaries are narrower still, but there are so many in parallel that their total resistance is lower than that of the arterioles.
Large arteries are wide, so little pressure is lost along them.
Pressure is already low in the veins, and falls only a little more.

questions.q: The arterioles supplying one organ dilate. How does the pressure profile through that organ change?
options: Less pressure is lost across them, so capillary pressure rises
More pressure is lost across the arterioles, so capillary pressure falls
Aortic pressure doubles
Nothing changes: arteriole size does not affect pressure

why.correct: Wider arterioles have much lower resistance (it depends on radius to the fourth power), so less pressure is used up crossing them. More pressure reaches the capillaries and more blood flows through the organ.
options: Right: lower resistance, smaller pressure drop, higher pressure downstream.
That is what constriction does: narrower arterioles use up more pressure.
One organ's arterioles barely change total resistance; the aorta's pressure stays about the same.
Radius is the most powerful control on resistance, and resistance sets how much pressure is lost.

graphs.title: Flow velocity vs cross-sectional area
graphs.intro: The same volume of blood, about 83 mL each second at rest, passes through every level of the circuit. The top panel shows the total cross-sectional area of all the vessels at each level; the bottom shows how fast the blood moves there.
graphs.alt: Two panels over the vessel types from aorta to venae cavae. Top: total cross-sectional area, tiny in the aorta (3 square centimeters), rising to a peak of about 3,000 in the capillaries and falling back to about 8 in the venae cavae. Bottom: mean velocity, highest in the aorta at about 28 centimeters per second, near zero in the capillaries, and rising to about 10 in the venae cavae: the mirror image of the area.

questions.q: Read the total cross-sectional area of all the capillaries.
questions.why: About 3,000 cm², about 1,000 times the aorta's 3 cm². Each capillary is tiny, but there are billions of them side by side.

questions.q: Read the mean velocity of blood in the aorta.
questions.why: About 28 cm/s. Velocity = flow ÷ area = 83 cm³/s ÷ 3 cm² ≈ 28 cm/s. (With each beat it surges much higher, then slows.)

questions.q: Where does blood move most slowly?
options: In the capillaries
In the aorta
In the venae cavae
In the large arteries

why.correct: Velocity equals flow divided by total area. The capillaries have the largest total area, so blood crawls through them, at about 0.03 cm/s (0.3 mm/s). That slow passage gives time for exchange.
options: Right: the biggest total area gives the slowest velocity.
The aorta has the smallest area, so blood moves fastest there.
The venae cavae have a small total area, so blood speeds up again as it returns.
Large arteries have little total area compared with the capillaries, so blood moves quickly through them.

questions.q: During exercise the heart pumps twice as much blood each minute, and the vessel areas stay the same. How does the velocity curve change?
options: Velocity doubles at every level, and it is still lowest in the capillaries
Velocity rises only in the aorta
Velocity in the capillaries rises above the aorta's
It does not change

why.correct: The same flow passes every level, so doubling it doubles the velocity everywhere. The shape of the curve is set by the areas, which have not changed.
options: Right: velocity = flow ÷ area, and only flow changed.
Every level carries the full flow in series, so every velocity rises.
The capillaries still have by far the largest total area, so they stay slowest.
More flow through the same area means faster blood.

graphs.title: Pressures along a capillary
graphs.intro: A typical capillary in the skin of your hand. The lines show the pressure pushing fluid out and the oncotic pull holding it in, in both the classic textbook picture and the revised Starling principle.
graphs.alt: Pressure in millimeters of mercury along a capillary from the arteriole end to the venule end. Capillary hydrostatic pressure falls in a straight line from 35 to 15. A flat dashed line at 25 is the plasma colloid osmotic pressure of the classic picture, crossing the hydrostatic line halfway. A third line, the effective inward pull across the glycocalyx, stays at 23 for the first half, then falls to 13, always just below the hydrostatic pressure.

series.label: effective inward pull across the glycocalyx

questions.q: Read the capillary hydrostatic pressure at the venule end.
questions.why: About 15 mm Hg, down from 35 at the arteriole end: blood loses pressure as it flows against the capillary's own resistance.

questions.q: At the arteriole end, work out the net pressure pushing fluid out: hydrostatic pressure minus the effective inward pull.
questions.why: 35 − 23 = 12 mm Hg outward. The effective pull is nearly the full plasma oncotic pressure, because the fluid just beneath the glycocalyx is kept almost protein-free by the outward flow.

questions.q: In the revised Starling picture, what happens to fluid in the venule half of the capillary at steady state?
options: It keeps filtering out, slowly
Most of it is reabsorbed into the blood
No fluid moves at all
It filters out faster than at the arteriole end

why.correct: The effective inward pull falls to stay just below hydrostatic pressure, so the net push stays slightly outward. If fluid began to flow in, protein would build up beneath the glycocalyx within minutes and stop it. For your exam: many courses still teach net reabsorption at the venule end, where the classic oncotic line lies above hydrostatic pressure.
options: Right: filtration slows but continues to the venule end.
That is the classic picture, which exams may still expect. Measurements show reabsorption does not last at steady state in most tissues.
Hydrostatic pressure still exceeds the effective pull, so fluid does move, slowly.
The gap between the lines is smaller near the venule end, so filtration is slower there.

questions.q: Liver disease lowers plasma albumin, and plasma oncotic pressure falls to about 15 mm Hg. How do the lines shift, and what happens to filtration?
options: The inward pull drops and filtration rises
Hydrostatic pressure falls to match, so nothing changes
The inward pull rises, so fluid is reabsorbed
No change, because albumin never crosses the wall anyway

why.correct: Albumin supplies most of plasma's oncotic pressure. With less of it, the pull holding fluid in falls all along the capillary, and the gap below hydrostatic pressure widens. Net filtration rises, and when it outpaces the drainage route, fluid collects between the cells as edema.
options: Right: a lower oncotic line means more filtration.
Hydrostatic pressure comes from the heart and arterioles, not from albumin, so it does not follow.
Less albumin means less oncotic pull, not more.
Albumin matters precisely because it stays in the plasma: that is what creates the pull.

questions.q: After sudden blood loss, the arterioles constrict and capillary hydrostatic pressure drops to 20 mm Hg at the arteriole end. What happens to fluid at first?
options: Fluid briefly moves into the blood
Filtration speeds up
Fluid is reabsorbed steadily for days
Nothing changes

why.correct: Hydrostatic pressure now lies below the effective inward pull along the whole capillary, so fluid moves into the blood. Within minutes, protein builds up beneath the glycocalyx and the inflow stops. After that, the capillaries keep filtering less than before while the separate drainage route keeps returning fluid at its old rate, so the plasma keeps gaining fluid for hours.
options: Right: a real inflow, but it stops within minutes.
Lower hydrostatic pressure means less push outward, not more.
Reabsorption shuts itself off as protein collects beneath the glycocalyx.
The pressure balance has reversed, so fluid does move.

graphs.title: Pressures during one quiet breath
graphs.intro: One quiet breath of 4 seconds: the change in lung volume (top) and the alveolar and intrapleural pressures, written relative to the air outside (bottom). 0 means equal to atmospheric pressure.
graphs.alt: Two panels sharing a time axis from 0 to 4 seconds. Top: lung volume rises smoothly from 0 to 0.5 liters at 2 seconds and falls back to 0 at 4 seconds. Bottom: alveolar pressure dips to −1 millimeter of mercury at 1 second, returns to 0 at 2 seconds, rises to +1 at 3 seconds and returns to 0 at 4 seconds. Intrapleural pressure starts at −4, falls to about −6 by 1 second and stays near −6 until the end of the breath in, then rises back to about −4 by 3 seconds, staying below atmospheric throughout. The gap between the two pressure curves tracks lung volume.

questions.q: Read the lowest alveolar pressure during the breath in.
questions.why: About −1 mm Hg, at 1 second. By Boyle’s law, the enlarging alveoli lower their own pressure just below atmospheric, and that small gradient drives air in.

questions.q: Read the intrapleural pressure at the end of the breath in, at 2 seconds.
questions.why: About −6 mm Hg. As the chest wall moves out, it pulls harder on the pleural fluid film, and its pressure falls from −4 to −6.

questions.q: Transpulmonary pressure is alveolar pressure minus intrapleural pressure. Read both at 2 seconds and work it out.
questions.why: 0 − (−6) = 6 mm Hg, up from 0 − (−4) = 4 mm Hg at the start. The larger transpulmonary pressure is what holds the lungs at their larger size at the end of the breath in.

questions.q: How much air has entered the lungs by the end of the breath in?
questions.why: About 0.5 L, a typical quiet breath. Volume peaks at 2 seconds, the moment alveolar pressure is back to 0 and flow stops.

questions.q: When is air flowing into the lungs fastest?
options: Around 1 s, when alveolar pressure is lowest
At 2 s, when lung volume is largest
At 0 s, as the muscles begin to contract
Around 3 s, when alveolar pressure is highest

why.correct: Flow = ΔP ÷ R, so inflow is fastest when alveolar pressure is furthest below atmospheric. That is also when the volume curve rises most steeply. The largest volume comes later, at 2 seconds, once flow has stopped.
options: Right: the steepest gradient gives the fastest flow.
At 2 s the gradient is gone, so flow has just stopped, even though volume is at its peak.
At the very start, alveolar pressure is still 0, so no gradient drives air in yet.
At 3 s alveolar pressure is above atmospheric, so air is flowing out fastest, not in.

questions.q: During which part of the breath is alveolar pressure above atmospheric pressure?
options: Expiration, from 2 to 4 s
Inspiration, from 0 to 2 s
Never: it stays below atmospheric throughout
Only at the instants when flow stops

why.correct: As the stretched lungs recoil, alveolar volume falls, and by Boyle’s law alveolar pressure rises to about +1 mm Hg, pushing air out. It is intrapleural pressure, not alveolar, that stays below atmospheric the whole time.
options: Right: recoil squeezes the alveolar air above atmospheric.
During inspiration alveolar pressure dips below atmospheric; that is what draws air in.
That is true of intrapleural pressure. Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric in expiration.
When flow stops, alveolar pressure equals atmospheric: 0, not above it.

questions.q: A stab wound lets outside air into the pleural cavity. What happens to the intrapleural pressure line?
options: It rises to about 0 and stays there
It falls further, to below −8 mm Hg
It keeps its shape, because the lung keeps it negative
It swings more widely with each breath

why.correct: The pleural cavity now opens to the outside air, so its pressure equals atmospheric. Transpulmonary pressure falls to about 0, nothing holds the lung open, and it collapses.
options: Right: intrapleural pressure equals atmospheric once air gets in.
Air from outside raises the pressure; it cannot pull it lower.
The negative pressure came from the lung and chest wall pulling on a sealed fluid film. Once the seal breaks, it is lost.
With the seal broken, chest movements no longer change the pressure in the cavity much.

questions.q: Scar tissue halves the lungs’ compliance. Starting from the same −4 mm Hg, how must the intrapleural pressure line change for the same 0.5 L breath?
options: It must dip twice as far, to about −8 mm Hg
It dips less, to about −5 mm Hg
It does not change; only alveolar pressure changes
It rises above atmospheric

why.correct: Compliance = ΔV ÷ ΔP. With half the compliance, the same 0.5 L needs twice the rise in transpulmonary pressure: 4 mm Hg instead of 2, from 4 to 8. Alveolar pressure still ends at 0, so intrapleural pressure must fall to −8. The breathing muscles pull twice as hard.
options: Right: half the compliance, twice the pressure change.
A smaller dip would inflate stiff lungs even less.
Alveolar pressure swings depend on airflow and airway resistance, which have not changed. The extra work shows up in the intrapleural pressure.
A pressure above atmospheric around the lungs would squeeze them, not inflate them.

graphs.title: Lung volumes and capacities (spirogram)
graphs.intro: A healthy young man breathes quietly, takes the deepest breath he can, blows out as far as he can, then breathes quietly again. The trace shows the total volume of air in his lungs.
graphs.alt: Lung volume in milliliters against time in seconds. Quiet breaths swing between 2,400 and 2,900. At about 12 seconds the deepest breath in reaches 5,900; at about 18 seconds the fullest breath out falls to 1,200; then quiet breaths resume between 2,400 and 2,900.

questions.q: Read the tidal volume: the volume of one quiet breath, from its bottom to its top.
questions.why: Each quiet breath swings from 2,400 to 2,900 mL: 500 mL.

questions.q: Read the inspiratory reserve volume: the extra air breathed in from the top of a quiet breath to the top of the deepest breath.
questions.why: 5,900 − 2,900 = 3,000 mL, the largest of the four volumes.

questions.q: Read the vital capacity: from the top of the deepest breath in to the bottom of the fullest breath out.
questions.why: 5,900 − 1,200 = 4,700 mL. Vital capacity is tidal volume plus both reserve volumes: 500 + 3,000 + 1,200.

questions.q: Read the functional residual capacity: the air still in the lungs at the end of a quiet breath out.
questions.why: About 2,400 mL: the expiratory reserve volume (1,200) plus the residual volume (1,200). It is where the inward recoil of the lungs balances the outward spring of the chest wall.

questions.q: Which part of this trace could a spirometer alone never measure?
options: The residual volume
The tidal volume of each quiet breath
The expiratory reserve volume
The inspiratory reserve volume

why.correct: A spirometer measures only air that crosses the mouthpiece. The residual volume never leaves the lungs, so it, and every capacity that includes it (FRC and total lung capacity), needs another test such as helium dilution or a body box.
options: Right: residual volume never passes the mouthpiece.
Every quiet breath passes through the mouthpiece, so the spirometer records it directly.
The expiratory reserve volume is breathed out, so it crosses the mouthpiece and can be measured.
This extra air is breathed in through the mouthpiece and recorded.

questions.q: Years of airway obstruction trap air: residual volume rises to 2,400 mL while total lung capacity stays about the same. How does the trace change?
options: Quiet breaths ride higher, the fullest breath out stops at 2,400 mL, and vital capacity shrinks
The whole trace sits lower, and vital capacity grows
Only the quiet breaths get deeper
The deepest breath in climbs above 5,900 mL, so vital capacity grows larger

why.correct: Narrowed airways close early during breath out and trap air, so residual volume and FRC rise. With total lung capacity unchanged, the space left for vital capacity shrinks: 5,900 − 2,400 = 3,500 mL.
options: Right: more air trapped, less air movable.
Air trapping raises the bottom of the trace; it does not lower it.
The problem is air that cannot get out, so the fullest breath out stops higher; quiet breaths do not simply deepen.
Total lung capacity stays about the same here, so the top of the deepest breath does not rise, and vital capacity falls.

questions.q: Fibrosis stiffens the lungs and every volume shrinks: total lung capacity falls to about 4,000 mL. How does the trace change?
options: Every volume shrinks; the peak is about 4,000 mL
The deepest breath in goes higher than before, because the lungs are firm
The fullest breath out stops higher because air is trapped
Only the breathing rate changes; the volumes stay the same

why.correct: Stiff lungs cannot expand fully, so the top of the deepest breath falls, and the whole trace shrinks: vital capacity is about 3,100 mL here. A low total lung capacity is what defines restriction.
options: Right: a smaller total lung capacity, and every volume shrinks.
Stiff lungs expand less, not more.
Air trapping belongs to obstructive disease. In restriction the airways are open.
Fibrosis changes how far the lungs can stretch, so the volumes themselves shrink.

graphs.title: Forced breath out: FEV1 and FVC
graphs.intro: Three people breathe in as deeply as they can and blow out as hard and fast as they can. Each curve shows the volume blown out against time.
graphs.alt: Volume breathed out in liters against time from 0 to 6 seconds, with a line at 1 second. Normal: 4.0 liters at 1 second, 5.0 in total. Patient A: a slow, gradual curve, 1.6 liters at 1 second, 3.9 in total. Patient B: a fast curve that levels off early, 2.2 liters at 1 second, 2.5 in total.

x.label: Time from start of forced breath out

questions.q: Read the normal person’s FEV1: the volume blown out in the first second.
questions.why: About 4.0 L, which is 80% of this person’s FVC of 5.0 L. Healthy lungs empty fast.

questions.q: Read patient A’s FVC: the total volume blown out.
questions.why: About 3.9 L. Patient A can still blow out most of a normal volume; the problem is how slowly it comes out.

questions.q: Read patient A’s FEV1 and FVC, and work out the FEV1/FVC ratio.
questions.why: 1.6 ÷ 3.9 = 0.41, far below 0.70: air is leaving the lungs too slowly. Patient B’s ratio is 2.2 ÷ 2.5 = 0.88, normal or high even though the volume is small.

questions.q: Which person shows an obstructive pattern?
options: Patient A, whose FEV1/FVC is about 0.41
Patient B, whose FVC is the smallest
Both, because each has a smaller FVC than normal
Neither, because only a small FVC shows obstruction

why.correct: Obstruction narrows the airways, so air has trouble getting out: FEV1 falls far more than FVC and the ratio drops below 0.70. Patient B’s small volume that leaves quickly points to restriction instead.
options: Right: slow emptying, low ratio.
A small FVC with a normal or high ratio suggests restriction, not obstruction.
A small FVC alone does not show obstruction; the ratio does. Patient B’s is normal.
Obstruction is recognized by the ratio, not by the FVC.

questions.q: Patient A turns out to have asthma. Ten minutes after an albuterol inhaler relaxes the airway smooth muscle, the test is repeated. How does the curve change?
options: It rises and steepens: FEV1 and the ratio increase
It flattens further, as the relaxed airways fold shut
It drops to match patient B
It stays the same, because the FVC is fixed

why.correct: Albuterol, a beta-2 agonist, relaxes airway smooth muscle. The radius grows, resistance falls steeply (fourth-power rule), and air leaves faster: here FEV1 rises from 1.6 to 3.3 L and the ratio from 0.41 to about 0.72. Asthma largely reverses.
options: Right: wider airways empty faster.
Relaxing the smooth muscle opens the airways, so the curve improves.
Patient B’s curve reflects small lungs, not narrow airways.
The drug changes how fast air leaves, and air trapping eases, so FVC can rise too.

questions.q: Suppose instead that patient A’s obstruction comes from decades of smoking. After albuterol, FEV1/FVC is still well below 0.70. What does the repeated curve look like?
options: Almost unchanged: the obstruction persists despite the drug
The same as the normal curve
Higher than the normal curve
The same as patient B’s curve

why.correct: COPD is confirmed when FEV1/FVC stays below 0.70 after a drug that opens the airways. In emphysema the airways collapse for lack of elastic support, and in chronic bronchitis mucus and thickened walls narrow them; relaxing smooth muscle fixes neither.
options: Right: persistent obstruction is what defines COPD.
A return to normal would mean the obstruction reversed, which fits asthma, not COPD.
No drug makes lungs empty faster than healthy ones.
Patient B’s shape comes from small, stiff lungs, not from narrowed airways.

graphs.title: PO2 and PCO2 along the path
graphs.intro: The partial pressures of oxygen and carbon dioxide at each stop from the air to the tissues and back, at rest at sea level. Each gas moves downhill on its own partial pressure.
graphs.alt: Partial pressure in millimeters of mercury at six stops. PO2: dry air 159, air in the airways 150, alveolar air 100, arterial blood 95, tissue fluid 40, venous blood 40. PCO2: dry air 0.3, air in the airways 0.3, alveolar air 40, arterial blood 40, tissue fluid 46, venous blood 46.

questions.q: Read the PO2 of alveolar air.
questions.why: About 100 mm Hg. Each breath adds fresh air to a much larger volume already in the alveoli, while blood takes oxygen out all the time, so the value settles well below the 150 of breathed-in air.

questions.q: Read the PCO2 of venous blood returning to the lungs.
questions.why: About 46 mm Hg: blood has picked up carbon dioxide from the tissues, where cells make it in aerobic respiration.

questions.q: Blood arriving in the pulmonary capillaries has the PO2 of venous blood. How large is the PO2 gradient from alveolar air to that blood?
questions.why: 100 − 40 = 60 mm Hg. The carbon dioxide gradient the other way is only 46 − 40 = 6 mm Hg, but carbon dioxide is about 20 times more soluble, so it crosses at least as readily: 6 × 20 = 120 against 60 × 1.

questions.q: Between which two neighboring stops does PO2 fall the most?
options: Arterial blood to tissue fluid
Dry air to air in the airways
Air in the airways to alveolar air
Alveolar air to arterial blood

why.correct: From about 95 to 40 mm Hg, a fall of 55: cells use oxygen continuously, so tissue PO2 stays low, and oxygen leaves the blood down that steep gradient. In working muscle the drop is larger still.
options: Right: the largest fall, where cells use the oxygen.
Adding water vapor lowers PO2 by only about 9 mm Hg, from 159 to 150.
A real drop, from 150 to 100, but 5 mm Hg smaller than the one in the tissues.
Only about 5 mm Hg, from a little venous blood mixing in and uneven V/Q.

questions.q: At 4,300 m, the PO2 of air in the airways falls to about 85 mm Hg. How does the PO2 line change?
options: Lower at every stop from the air to the blood
Only the dry-air point falls; the alveoli stay at 100
It rises, because the air is thinner
It does not change; only the PCO2 line moves

why.correct: The oxygen percentage is unchanged, but the total pressure is lower, so every downstream PO2 starts from a lower value. Alveolar and arterial PO2 fall to about 50, and less oxygen is pushed into the blood.
options: Right: a lower start lowers every step.
The alveoli are filled with that same low-PO2 air, so they cannot stay at 100.
Thinner air means a lower total pressure, and so a lower partial pressure of oxygen.
The oxygen line is what changes most. Carbon dioxide in air is near zero either way.

questions.q: Alveolar ventilation falls to two thirds of normal while carbon dioxide production stays the same. How does the PCO2 line change?
options: It rises from the alveoli onward
Alveolar and arterial PCO2 fall, because less air is breathed
It stays at 40: only oxygen depends on ventilation
Only the dry-air point changes

why.correct: The alveolar value is a balance between carbon dioxide added by blood and carbon dioxide washed out by fresh air. Less ventilation washes out less, so alveolar PCO2 rises (here to about 60 mm Hg), and arterial blood leaves the lungs matching it. Alveolar PO2 falls at the same time.
options: Right: less washout, more carbon dioxide left behind.
Breathing less removes less carbon dioxide, so it rises.
Carbon dioxide leaves the body only by ventilation, so it depends on ventilation more directly than oxygen does.
Outside air is unaffected; the change is in the alveoli and the blood.

graphs.title: The oxygen–hemoglobin dissociation curve
graphs.intro: How saturated hemoglobin is at each PO2, for adult blood at pH 7.4, a PCO2 of 40 mm Hg and 37 °C.
graphs.alt: Hemoglobin saturation in percent against PO2 from 0 to 100 millimeters of mercury. The S-shaped curve rises slowly at first, then steeply between about 10 and 50: 35 percent at 20, 50 percent at 27, 75 percent at 40. It flattens above 60: 90 percent at 60 and 98 percent at 100.

questions.q: Read the saturation at a PO2 of 40 mm Hg, typical of resting tissue.
questions.why: About 75%. Blood leaving resting tissue still carries three quarters of its load, a reserve for exercise.

questions.q: Read the P50: the PO2 at which hemoglobin is 50% saturated.
questions.why: About 27 mm Hg for normal adult blood. P50 is the single number that says where the curve sits: a higher P50 means a right shift.

questions.q: Read the saturation at a PO2 of 60 mm Hg.
questions.why: About 90%. Clinicians treat an SpO2 of about 90% as a warning line: below a PO2 of 60, small further falls cause large drops in saturation.

questions.q: Over which range does a fall in PO2 change saturation least?
options: Between 60 and 100 mm Hg
Between 10 and 50 mm Hg
Below 10 mm Hg
Saturation falls by the same amount everywhere

why.correct: The top of the curve is almost flat, so blood still loads nearly fully in the lungs even when alveolar PO2 falls quite a lot, as at moderate altitude or in mild lung disease.
options: Right: the flat loading zone.
This is the steep part, where small falls in PO2 release large amounts of oxygen.
The curve still rises here; saturation is low but changing.
Cooperative binding makes the curve S-shaped, not straight.

questions.q: Blood arrives at exercising muscle 98% saturated, and the muscle’s PO2 is 20 mm Hg. How many percentage points of saturation does the blood give up?
questions.why: Saturation at 20 mm Hg is about 35%, so 98 − 35 = 63 points, nearly two thirds of the load, against 98 − 75 = 23 at rest. The steep middle of the curve releases oxygen as tissue PO2 falls, with no signal needed.

questions.q: Blood reaches warm, acidic muscle full of carbon dioxide. How does the curve shift?
options: Right: lower saturation at each tissue PO2, so more oxygen is released
Left: higher saturation at each PO2, so less is released
Down: the top of the curve falls to about 60%
It does not shift; only PO2 matters

why.correct: Carbon dioxide and H+ hold hemoglobin in its tense, low-affinity shape (the Bohr effect), and heat weakens the oxygen–heme bond. P50 rises to about 38, and at a PO2 of 40, saturation falls from 75% to about 53%, nearly doubling the oxygen released. The top still loads to about 94%.
options: Right: lower affinity, more unloading.
A left shift is caused by the opposite conditions: less carbon dioxide, fewer H+, cooler blood.
A lower top means sites blocked, as with carbon monoxide. These factors lower affinity, not the number of sites.
Affinity changes with carbon dioxide, H+, temperature and 2,3-BPG, and the curve moves with it.

questions.q: Where does the curve for fetal hemoglobin lie?
options: To the left, with a P50 near 19 mm Hg
To the right, with a P50 near 38 mm Hg
Exactly on the adult curve
Lower, with a top near 60%

why.correct: Fetal hemoglobin has gamma chains, which bind 2,3-BPG weakly, so it stays in its high-affinity shape more easily. At any low PO2 it is more saturated than adult hemoglobin, so oxygen passes from maternal to fetal blood.
options: Right: higher affinity, a left shift.
A right shift would make fetal blood give oxygen away, not take it from the mother.
Its different chains give it a different affinity.
Fetal hemoglobin still loads fully; it just holds oxygen more tightly.

questions.q: Carbon monoxide occupies 30% of hemoglobin’s sites. How does the curve of oxygen actually carried on hemoglobin change?
options: Top falls to about 70%; it shifts left
It shifts right, so more oxygen is released
Its top falls to about 70%, and it shifts right
It does not change, because PO2 stays normal

why.correct: Sites holding carbon monoxide cannot carry oxygen, so even at a high PO2 only about 70% of sites carry it. Carbon monoxide also holds each molecule in its relaxed shape, a left shift, so the oxygen that is carried comes off less in the tissues. A standard pulse oximeter misses both.
options: Right: fewer sites, held more tightly.
Carbon monoxide raises affinity; it shifts the curve left, not right.
The top does fall, but the shift is to the left.
PO2 measures dissolved oxygen, which is normal. The hemoglobin curve still changes.

graphs.title: Ventilation and arterial PCO2
graphs.intro: How much you breathe each minute as your arterial PCO2 is raised, with oxygen held normal. Shapes are approximate.
graphs.alt: Ventilation in liters per minute against arterial PCO2 from 35 to 55 millimeters of mercury. The line rises steeply: about 6 liters per minute at 40, 12 at 45, 20 at 50 and 28 at 55.

questions.q: Read the ventilation at a normal arterial PCO2 of 40 mm Hg.
questions.why: About 6 L/min, a typical resting value: roughly 12 breaths of 500 mL.

questions.q: Arterial PCO2 rises to 45 mm Hg. Read the ventilation.
questions.why: About 12 L/min: a rise of only 5 mm Hg roughly doubles ventilation. Carbon dioxide, acting mostly through the central chemoreceptors, is the main drive to breathe.

questions.q: At what arterial PCO2 does ventilation reach 20 L/min?
questions.why: About 50 mm Hg. Reading a graph backward, from the y axis to the x axis, works the same way as forward.

questions.q: In which range is a person hypercapnic?
options: Arterial PCO2 above 45 mm Hg
Arterial PCO2 from 35 to 45 mm Hg
Arterial PCO2 below 35 mm Hg
Whenever ventilation is above 6 L/min

why.correct: Hypercapnia means a high arterial PCO2, above the normal 35 to 45 mm Hg. It is defined by carbon dioxide, not by how much the person is breathing.
options: Right: above 45 mm Hg.
This is the normal range.
Below 35 mm Hg is hypocapnia, the result of hyperventilation.
Ventilation can be high with a normal PCO2, as in exercise. The PCO2 decides.

questions.q: An opioid overdose depresses the respiratory centers. How does the line change?
options: It flattens: a weaker response
It steepens
It shifts up: more ventilation at every PCO2
It does not change, because the chemoreceptors still work

why.correct: The chemoreceptors still sense the rise, but the depressed respiratory centers turn their signal into much less breathing. PCO2 climbs, and the person hypoventilates.
options: Right: a weak response to carbon dioxide.
A steeper line would mean a stronger response, the opposite of depression.
More ventilation at every PCO2 would lower carbon dioxide; opioids raise it.
Sensing is not enough: the control center must act on the signal.

questions.q: Acid from another source, such as very hard exercise, lowers blood pH while PCO2 is held steady. How does the line change?
options: It shifts up and left: more ventilation at every PCO2
It shifts down and right: less ventilation at every PCO2
It flattens
It does not change: only carbon dioxide affects breathing

why.correct: The carotid bodies respond to a fall in arterial pH from any cause, within seconds. That adds drive at every PCO2, so the whole line moves up. Hydrogen ions cross the blood–brain barrier poorly, so the central chemoreceptors notice this acid only slowly.
options: Right: the carotid bodies add drive.
Acid adds drive to breathe; it does not remove it.
The response to carbon dioxide is not weakened; extra drive is added on top.
The peripheral chemoreceptors respond to low pH whatever its cause.

questions.q: A person with severe long-term lung disease has had a high PCO2 for months, and the central chemoreceptors have adapted. How does the line change?
options: It flattens and shifts right
It steepens and shifts left, like a stronger response
It shifts up: more ventilation at every PCO2
It does not change: adaptation takes years

why.correct: Over a day or two, bicarbonate in the cerebrospinal fluid is adjusted upward, bringing its pH back toward normal. The central chemoreceptors then respond less to the lasting high PCO2, so each mm Hg drives less breathing.
options: Right: adaptation blunts the response.
Adaptation weakens the response; it does not strengthen it.
More ventilation at every PCO2 would lower the PCO2, which is not what happens in these patients.
The central chemoreceptors adapt over a day or two.

graphs.title: Ventilation and arterial PO2
graphs.intro: How much you breathe each minute as arterial PO2 falls, with PCO2 held at 40 mm Hg. Shapes are approximate.
graphs.alt: Ventilation in liters per minute against arterial PO2 from 30 to 100 millimeters of mercury. The curve is nearly flat, about 6 liters per minute, from 100 down to about 60, then rises steeply: about 9.5 at 50, 14.5 at 40 and 26 at 30.

questions.q: Read the ventilation at a normal arterial PO2 of 95 mm Hg.
questions.why: About 6 L/min, the resting value.

questions.q: Read the ventilation at an arterial PO2 of 40 mm Hg.
questions.why: About 14.5 L/min, well over twice the resting value. Below about 60 mm Hg the carotid bodies’ firing rises steeply, and the respiratory centers drive deeper, faster breathing. At this PO2 hemoglobin is on the steep part of its curve, so the blood is losing oxygen content fast.

questions.q: Below about which arterial PO2 does ventilation start to rise steeply?
options: About 60 mm Hg
About 90 mm Hg
About 35 mm Hg
It rises steadily all the way from 100

why.correct: The carotid bodies’ own response is shaped this way: their firing rises only a little as PO2 falls from 100 to about 60 mm Hg, then steeply below that. Over the flat range hemoglobin stays about 90% saturated or more, so little oxygen is lost. Minute to minute, carbon dioxide, not oxygen, sets your breathing.
options: Right: about 60 mm Hg.
At 90 mm Hg the curve is still flat.
The rise is already steep well above 35 mm Hg.
The curve is nearly flat from 100 down to 60.

questions.q: A woman with severe anemia has a normal arterial PO2 of 95 mm Hg but carries far less oxygen per liter of blood. Where does her breathing sit on this graph?
options: On the flat part, near 6 L/min: her carotid bodies sense a normal PO2
High on the steep part, as if her PO2 were 40
Above the whole curve, because her tissues are short of oxygen
At zero, because anemia stops breathing

why.correct: The carotid bodies sense the partial pressure of oxygen, not the amount the blood carries. In anemia, and in carbon monoxide poisoning, arterial PO2 is normal, so the carotid bodies are not stimulated much and breathing barely rises.
options: Right: PO2, not oxygen content, drives the carotid bodies.
Her PO2 is 95, not 40. The sensors respond to partial pressure.
No sensor in this loop measures oxygen content or tissue oxygen.
Anemia does not affect the respiratory centers.

questions.q: Both carotid bodies have been removed. How does the curve change?
options: Nearly flat all the way down
It rises even more steeply, because the central chemoreceptors take over
It shifts to the right
It is unchanged, because the aortic bodies do the job

why.correct: The carotid bodies are the only sensors that drive breathing up when oxygen falls; the aortic bodies play a small part in adults, and the central chemoreceptors do not sense oxygen. Without them, the response to low oxygen is nearly lost.
options: Right: the low-oxygen response is lost.
Central chemoreceptors sense hydrogen ions made from carbon dioxide, not oxygen.
A right shift would still mean a response. Here there is almost none.
The aortic bodies contribute little to breathing in adults.

graphs.title: Neuron action potential with channel states and refractory periods
graphs.intro: The top panel is the voltage at the trigger zone of an axon; a stimulus arrives at 0.5 ms. The bottom panel shows, for the same moments, how many voltage-gated sodium and potassium channels are open, as a share of the most that open.
graphs.alt: Two panels over 6 milliseconds. Top: membrane potential rises from −70 mV, crosses threshold at −55 mV near 0.95 ms, peaks near +30 mV at about 1.45 ms, falls back through −70 mV at about 2.25 ms, dips to about −80 mV near 2.9 ms, and returns to −70 mV by about 5.5 ms. Bottom: sodium channels open sharply, peaking near 1.3 ms, and are nearly all shut again by 2 ms; potassium channels open later and more slowly, peaking near 2.2 ms, and close gradually by about 5 ms.

questions.q: Read the lowest voltage the membrane reaches after the spike.
questions.why: About −80 mV. The delayed potassium channels are slow to close, so potassium keeps leaving and pulls the membrane below rest, toward potassium’s equilibrium potential of about −90 mV.

questions.q: Read how long the rising phase takes, from threshold (−55 mV) to the peak. Give your answer in ms.
questions.why: About 0.5 ms: threshold is crossed near 0.95 ms and the peak comes near 1.45 ms. The rise is so fast because it is positive feedback: each bit of depolarization opens more sodium activation gates.
