questions.q: Name the stretch, from threshold through most of the falling phase, during which no stimulus of any strength can start a second action potential.
options: Absolute refractory period
Relative refractory period
Afterhyperpolarization
Rest

why.correct: Throughout this stretch every sodium channel is either open or inactivated. An inactivated channel cannot open until the membrane repolarizes, so there are no ready channels for a stimulus to open.
options: Right: complete, without exception.
In the relative refractory period some sodium channels have reset, so a stronger-than-normal stimulus can fire the axon. That comes later, as the membrane repolarizes.
The afterhyperpolarization is the dip below rest after the spike, when potassium channels are still open; it overlaps the relative refractory period, not the absolute one.
At rest every sodium channel is closed and ready, so a normal stimulus can fire the axon.

questions.q: From late in the falling phase through the dip below rest, a second action potential can fire, but only with a stronger-than-normal stimulus. Name this stretch.
options: Relative refractory period
Absolute refractory period
The rising phase, when sodium rushes in
A graded potential sized to its stimulus

why.correct: Some sodium channels have reset, so a spike is possible. But fewer are ready than at rest, and the still-open potassium channels hold the membrane below rest, farther from threshold, so the stimulus must be stronger.
options: Right: harder than normal, compared with rest, but not impossible.
During the absolute refractory period no stimulus works, because no sodium channels are ready. Here some are.
The rising phase is the fast climb from threshold to the peak, driven by sodium entry.
A graded potential is a small change sized to its stimulus, not a period of reduced excitability.

questions.q: Compare the two panels during the falling phase, from the peak back down to −70 mV. What are the channels doing?
options: Sodium channels are inactivating while potassium channels are open
Sodium channels are open and potassium channels are closed
Both kinds of channel are closed, and the pump restores the voltage
Potassium channels are letting potassium flow into the axon

why.correct: The sodium curve drops steeply after its peak as the inactivation gates plug the pores, while the potassium curve climbs toward its maximum. Sodium entry stops and potassium leaves, so the membrane repolarizes.
options: Right: sodium inflow ends and potassium outflow takes over.
That describes the rising phase, when sodium rushes in before the delayed potassium channels have opened.
The bottom panel shows potassium channels near their most open here. The pump is slow and moves only a tiny share of the ions per spike.
Potassium is concentrated inside the axon, so it flows out. Losing positive charge is what makes the voltage fall.

questions.q: A toxin blocks the voltage-gated potassium channels; the leak channels still work. How does the action potential change?
options: It falls back more slowly, lasts longer and loses its dip below rest
It never starts, because potassium channels are needed to reach threshold
It peaks near +60 mV and then falls as usual
Nothing changes, because leak channels carry all the potassium

why.correct: The rise is sodium’s work and is unchanged. Normally the delayed potassium channels make the fall fast and carry the membrane below rest. With them blocked, only the slow leak and sodium inactivation bring the voltage down, so the spike is wider and there is no afterhyperpolarization.
options: Right: a slower fall, a wider spike and no dip.
Reaching threshold depends on sodium channels opening, not on potassium channels.
The peak is capped by sodium inactivation as well as by potassium channels opening, so it stays about the same.
The leak channels carry the resting potassium current, far too little to repolarize the membrane quickly.

graphs.title: How far a signal travels: myelinated vs unmyelinated axons
graphs.intro: Three axons start carrying an action potential at the same moment. Each line shows how far along its axon the signal has traveled. The slope of each line is its conduction velocity.
graphs.alt: Distance traveled in meters against time in milliseconds, from 0 to 40 ms. A steep line for a wide myelinated axon at 120 m/s reaches 1.2 m at 10 ms. A line for a myelinated axon at 50 m/s reaches 1.2 m at 24 ms. A nearly flat line for a thin unmyelinated axon at 1 m/s reaches only 0.04 m at 40 ms.

questions.q: Read how long the 50 m/s myelinated axon takes to carry the signal 1.0 m, the distance from foot to spinal cord.
questions.why: About 20 ms. Time = distance ÷ velocity = 1.0 m ÷ 50 m/s = 0.02 s. The unmyelinated axon would take a full second for the same distance, fifty times longer, which is why a sharp touch is felt before the dull ache.

questions.q: Read how far the 50 m/s signal has traveled at 10 ms.
questions.why: About 0.5 m: 50 m/s × 0.010 s = 0.5 m. In the same 10 ms the widest myelinated axon has carried its signal 1.2 m, and the unmyelinated one only 1 cm.

questions.q: Which line shows continuous conduction, where every patch of membrane must fire in turn?
options: The nearly flat line, 1 m/s
The steepest line, 120 m/s
The middle line, 50 m/s
All three, since every axon fires every patch

why.correct: In an unmyelinated axon every tiny patch must reach threshold and fire before the next can start, so the signal creeps along at about 0.5 to 2 m/s: the flattest slope.
options: Right: slow, patch by patch.
The steepest line is a wide myelinated axon, where only the nodes fire and a wide axon lets current spread farther inside.
At 50 m/s the axon must be myelinated: saltatory conduction.
Under myelin there are very few sodium channels, so those stretches do not fire; only the nodes do.

questions.q: Disease strips myelin along the whole 50 m/s axon, and it adds sodium channels along the bare membrane so it still conducts, continuously, at about 2 m/s. How does its line change?
options: Still straight from the origin, but much less steep
It becomes steeper, because bare membrane fires faster
It keeps its slope but starts several milliseconds later
It becomes a flat line at zero: nothing is conducted

why.correct: Distance grows steadily with time, so the line stays straight, but its slope is the new, lower velocity. At 2 m/s the signal covers only 0.08 m in 40 ms, and reaching 1 m would take 500 ms instead of 20.
options: Right: same start, a shallower slope.
Losing myelin slows conduction: current leaks through the bare wall and every patch must fire.
The signal still starts at time zero; what changes is how fast it covers ground.
A flat line would mean complete conduction block. This axon still conducts, just slowly.

graphs.title: Spatial and temporal summation at the trigger zone
graphs.intro: The membrane potential at a neuron’s trigger zone over 100 ms, during four experiments. Each EPSP is drawn as 5 mV and the IPSP as 3 mV, larger than real ones in the brain so they can be seen. Where the trace shoots off the top, the neuron fired an action potential.
graphs.alt: Membrane potential from −75 to −45 mV over 100 ms, with threshold marked at −55 mV. From 0 to 18 ms a single EPSP rises to −65 mV and fades. From 20 to 46 ms four EPSPs from one input arrive 3 ms apart and stack until the trace reaches −55 mV and shoots off the top. From 50 to 70 ms three EPSPs from different inputs arrive together, reach −55 mV at once and the trace shoots off the top. From 75 to 100 ms a single IPSP dips to −73 mV and fades back to −70.

questions.q: Read the highest membrane potential reached by the single EPSP in the first 18 ms.
questions.why: About −65 mV, 5 mV above rest and still 10 mV short of threshold, so it fades without firing the neuron. A real EPSP in the brain is usually under 1 mV: neuron-to-neuron synapses vote rather than command.

questions.q: Read the lowest membrane potential in the last experiment, after 75 ms.
questions.why: About −73 mV. The IPSP opens chloride channels; chloride flowing in hyperpolarizes the membrane a little, away from threshold.

questions.q: In experiment 2 (20 to 46 ms), a single presynaptic neuron fires four times in quick succession. What kind of summation brings the trigger zone to threshold?
options: Temporal summation
Spatial summation
An IPSP
The all-or-none rule

why.correct: Each EPSP begins before the last has faded, so they stack in time until the sum reaches −55 mV and the neuron fires.
options: Right: one input, repeated quickly.
Spatial summation adds EPSPs from several different inputs arriving at about the same time.
An IPSP moves the membrane away from threshold; every bump here is upward.
The all-or-none rule describes the action potential that fires once threshold is reached, not how the EPSPs add up to it.

questions.q: In experiment 3 (50 to 70 ms), three different presynaptic neurons, at different places on the cell, fire at the same moment. What kind of summation is this?
options: Spatial summation
Temporal summation
Divergence
A single large EPSP from one synapse

why.correct: EPSPs from different synapses arrive at the trigger zone together and add: 3 × 5 mV = 15 mV, exactly the step from −70 to −55 mV, so the neuron fires.
options: Right: several inputs at once.
Temporal summation is one input firing repeatedly; here three inputs fire once each.
Divergence is one neuron sending its signal to many; here many neurons converge on one.
Each synapse gives only a small EPSP; the size comes from adding three of them.

questions.q: Repeat experiment 3, but an inhibitory input fires at the same moment as the three excitatory ones. How does the trace change?
options: It peaks about 3 mV lower and stays below threshold
It reaches threshold sooner, because more inputs are active
It is unchanged, because an IPSP only acts on a neuron at rest
The neuron fires two action potentials instead of one

why.correct: EPSPs and IPSPs add algebraically: 3 × 5 − 3 = 12 mV, which takes the trigger zone only to −58 mV. It falls short of −55 mV, so no action potential fires.
options: Right: the IPSP subtracts from the sum.
An IPSP moves the membrane away from threshold, so reaching it takes more, not less.
Whatever the membrane is doing, the IPSP’s chloride current subtracts from the depolarization the EPSPs build.
Adding inhibition cannot add a spike. The sum is now below threshold.

questions.q: Repeat experiment 2, but the same four EPSPs arrive 6 ms apart instead of 3 ms apart. How does the trace change?
options: The EPSPs fade between arrivals and never reach threshold
It reaches threshold sooner, because each EPSP has more time to grow
Each EPSP becomes larger to make up for the longer gaps
Nothing changes, because the same four EPSPs still arrive in the end

why.correct: Temporal summation works only if each EPSP begins before the last has faded. With 6 ms gaps most of each one has decayed, so the stack tops out near −61.5 mV, well short of threshold.
options: Right: timing decides whether they stack.
Spreading the inputs out gives each EPSP more time to fade, so the sum is lower, not higher.
Each EPSP is set by the neurotransmitter released at its synapse, not by the gap before it.
Graded potentials fade within milliseconds, so the same inputs spread out in time add up to less.

graphs.title: A night of sleep (hypnogram)
graphs.intro: The sleep stages of a healthy young adult across one 8-hour night, as scored from the EEG. Higher on the graph is lighter; REM periods are drawn in color.
graphs.alt: A stepped line over 8 hours with five levels, from top to bottom: awake, REM, N1, N2 and N3. The sleeper passes from awake through N1 and N2 into N3 within half an hour, stays in N3 until about 1.1 hours, and has a short REM period at about 1.3 hours. The night repeats in cycles of about 90 minutes. N3 appears in the first three cycles and shrinks each time, then disappears. REM periods lengthen from about 10 minutes in the first cycle to about 48 minutes in the last, which ends with waking at about 7.7 hours.

questions.q: Read how many hours after falling asleep the first REM period begins.
questions.why: About 1.3 hours, roughly 80 minutes: the first cycle runs down through N1 and N2 into deep N3 and back up before the first, short REM period.

questions.q: Read how long the last REM period lasts, from about 6.9 hours to waking. Give your answer in minutes.
questions.why: About 0.8 hours, or 48 minutes, compared with about 10 minutes for the first. REM periods lengthen toward morning, which is why you often wake from a dream.

questions.q: Name the stage the sleeper reaches at the lowest level of the graph, from about 0.45 to 1.1 hours.
options: N3, slow-wave sleep
REM sleep
N1
Awake

why.correct: N3 is the deepest stage: large, slow delta waves show huge numbers of cortical neurons swinging together, breathing and heart rate are slow and regular, and the sleeper is hardest to wake. It fills the early cycles.
options: Right: deep, slow-wave sleep.
REM sleep looks like waking on the EEG and comes at the end of each cycle, not at the bottom.
N1 is the light drift into sleep, lasting only a few minutes at the start.
The sleeper is awake only at the very start and at the end of the night.

questions.q: Look at the stretch from falling asleep (about 0.1 h) to the end of the first REM period (about 1.45 h). What is it, and about how long does it last?
options: One sleep cycle, about 90 minutes
One REM period, about 90 minutes
One sleep cycle, about 30 minutes
The whole of non-REM sleep for the night

why.correct: Each cycle passes from light non-REM sleep into N3, back up, and ends with a REM period. Cycles last about 90 minutes and repeat four to six times a night; this one lasts about 1.35 hours.
options: Right: a full cycle of about 90 minutes.
The REM period is only the short colored stretch at the end of the cycle.
The stretch spans about 1.35 hours, far longer than 30 minutes.
Non-REM sleep returns in every later cycle, so this is only the first of several.

questions.q: An alarm wakes the sleeper at 6 hours instead of letting them wake at 7.7. Compared with the full night, which state loses the most time?
options: REM sleep
N3, slow-wave sleep
N1
All stages lose about the same share

why.correct: N3 fills the first half of the night and is gone by the fourth cycle, so an early alarm cuts none of it. The longest REM periods come last, so the lost time is mostly REM: here about 60 of the night’s roughly 130 REM minutes.
options: Right: the end of the night is REM-rich.
N3 is concentrated in the first half of the night, all before 6 hours.
N1 fills only a few minutes, at sleep onset and after brief awakenings.
The stages are not spread evenly through the night: early cycles are N3-rich and later ones REM-rich.

graphs.title: Tonic and phasic sensory receptors
graphs.intro: A steady press is held on the skin from 1 to 4 seconds (top). Below it are the firing rates recorded from the sensory neurons of two kinds of sensory receptor under that press: a tonic (slowly adapting) one and a phasic (rapidly adapting) one.
graphs.alt: Two panels over 5 seconds. Top: pressure on the skin, zero until 1 s, then steady until 4 s, then zero. Bottom: firing rate. The tonic sensory receptor jumps to about 70 action potentials per second at 1 s and declines slowly to about 46 by 4 s, then stops. The phasic one fires a brief burst of about 85 at 1 s, falls silent within a quarter second while the press is held, and fires another brief burst of about 60 when the press ends at 4 s.

questions.q: Read the tonic sensory receptor’s firing rate two seconds into the press, at 3 s.
questions.why: About 48 per second, down only a little from its first 70. A tonic sensory receptor keeps reporting a steady stimulus for as long as it lasts, with only a small drop in frequency.

questions.q: During which part of the record is the phasic sensory receptor silent even though the press is still on?
options: While the press is held steady
As the press starts
As the press ends
At no time: it fires throughout

why.correct: A phasic sensory receptor signals change. Once the pressure stops changing, it adapts and falls silent, which is why you stop feeling a watch strap.
options: Right: steady pressure, no signal.
As the press starts it fires its strongest burst: the pressure is changing.
As the press is released it fires again, because removing the pressure is also a change.
Its line drops to zero within a quarter second of the press starting.

questions.q: The press is repeated at twice the pressure. How does the tonic line change while the press is held?
options: It runs higher throughout, with the same slow decline
It rises at first but reaches zero sooner
It does not change, because action potentials are all-or-none
It stays the same height, but each action potential is taller

why.correct: A firmer press opens more channels and depolarizes the ending more, which holds the trigger zone further above threshold, so the neuron fires more often. Strength is coded as frequency.
options: Right: stronger stimulus, higher frequency.
Adaptation in a tonic sensory receptor is slow whatever the strength; it keeps firing while the press lasts.
All-or-none fixes the size of each action potential, not how often they fire.
Each action potential is the same size. Only the rate, and the number of neurons firing, can change.

questions.q: Which line behaves like the nociceptors that keep reporting a sprained ankle for as long as the injury lasts?
options: The tonic line
The phasic line
The pressure line
Neither: pain sensors do not fire steadily

why.correct: Nociceptors are tonic: they keep firing while the damage lasts, so pain stays reported for as long as it matters.
options: Right: nociceptors, proprioceptors and the stretch sensors in artery walls are tonic.
Phasic sensory receptors, such as lamellated corpuscles, fall silent during a steady stimulus. An injury reported that way would be forgotten within a second.
The pressure line is the stimulus, not a sensory receptor’s response.
Nociceptors are among the most tonic sensory receptors of all.

graphs.title: Light absorbed by the three cone pigments and rhodopsin
graphs.intro: Each curve shows how strongly one photoreceptor pigment absorbs light of each wavelength, scaled so its own peak is 1. The peaks are measured values; the curves are drawn smooth and symmetrical for clarity.
graphs.alt: Relative absorbance from 0 to 1 against wavelength from 380 to 700 nanometers. Four overlapping bell-shaped curves peak at 420 nm (short-wavelength cones), 498 nm (rods), 534 nm (medium-wavelength cones) and 564 nm (long-wavelength cones).

questions.q: Read the wavelength that rhodopsin, the rod pigment, absorbs best.
questions.why: About 498 nm, blue-green light. That sits between the S and M cone peaks, which is part of why blue-green objects look relatively bright at dusk, when rods take over.

questions.q: Orange light of 600 nm reaches the retina. Which pigment absorbs it most strongly?
options: L cones
M cones
S cones
Rods

why.correct: At 600 nm the L curve is highest, the M curve lower and the S curve near zero. The brain reads the color from that ratio: strong L, some M, almost no S.
options: Right: L cones absorb it most.
M cones absorb 600 nm light, but less than L cones do; their curve has fallen well below its peak.
S cones barely absorb beyond about 500 nm.
Rods absorb little at 600 nm, and in bright light they are saturated anyway.

questions.q: Read the L cone pigment’s relative absorbance at 600 nm.
questions.why: About 0.7: the L pigment absorbs 600 nm light at roughly 70% of its best. Every cone type responds over a wide range, so a single cone cannot tell a dim light at its peak from a brighter light off its peak. Only comparing cone types gives color.

questions.q: In one form of red–green color blindness, the L pigment is altered so that its peak moves toward the M pigment’s. How does the L curve change?
options: It slides left, toward the M curve
It slides right, to longer wavelengths, away from M
It keeps its place but grows taller than the others
It disappears, leaving only the S and M curves

why.correct: With the L curve sitting almost on top of the M curve, reds, oranges and greens excite the two cone types in nearly the same ratio, so they look alike. In this form, called protanomaly, the altered pigment peaks within a few nanometers of M, at about 530 to 536 nm.
options: Right: it slides toward M.
Moving right would separate L from M further, which would sharpen red–green discrimination, not blunt it.
The height is scaled to 1 for every pigment; color vision depends on where the curves sit, not how tall they are drawn.
Losing the pigment entirely is another form of red–green color blindness, but this one alters it.

graphs.title: Dark adaptation
graphs.intro: After time in bright light, a person sits in total darkness while the dimmest light they can detect is measured. Sensitivity is plotted in log units: each unit is a tenfold gain, so 4 log units means lights 10,000 times dimmer can be seen.
graphs.alt: Sensitivity gained, in log units, against time in the dark from 0 to 35 minutes. A cone branch rises quickly to about 1.6 log units by 8 to 10 minutes and levels off. A rod branch takes over at about 8 minutes (the rod–cone break) and keeps rising to about 4 log units by 30 minutes.

questions.q: Read how much sensitivity has been gained after 20 minutes in the dark.
questions.why: About 3.6 log units, so lights about 4,000 times dimmer than at first can now be seen. Almost all of that gain comes from rods rebuilding rhodopsin.

questions.q: Read the time of the rod–cone break, where the rods take over.
questions.why: About 8 minutes. Before it, the cones, which recover within about 10 minutes, are the more sensitive; after it, the slowly recovering rods pull ahead.

questions.q: During which stretch is your sensitivity set by the cones?
options: Roughly the first 8 minutes
From about 8 minutes to the end of the record
Only after 30 minutes
The whole 35 minutes

why.correct: Cone pigment is rebuilt quickly, so cone sensitivity rises first, but it levels off low. For the first minutes the cones are still more sensitive than the bleached rods.
options: Right: the early, quick branch.
After the break the rods are more sensitive, so they set the threshold.
By 30 minutes the rods have long since taken over.
The curve has two branches: cones first, then rods.

questions.q: A person with a severe shortage of the dietary vitamin that retinal is made from sits in the dark. How does the curve change?
options: The rod branch rises far less, leaving poor night vision
The cone branch disappears, but the rod branch is normal
The whole curve reaches 4 log units sooner
Nothing changes, because retinal is recycled

why.correct: Without enough retinal, too little rhodopsin can be built, so the rods never become very sensitive: night blindness. Cones need less pigment to work in their bright-light range, so their branch suffers less at first.
options: Right: the rod branch is stunted.
Rods depend most on rhodopsin, so they are hit hardest; the rod branch is what fails.
Less pigment slows and limits adaptation; it cannot speed it up.
Retinal is recycled, but some is lost, and a long shortage leaves too little to rebuild rhodopsin.

graphs.title: The near point moves away with age
graphs.intro: The near point is the closest distance at which you can bring small print into focus. These are classic average values for eyes with normal distance vision. The near point is about 7 cm at age 10 and 10 cm at 20.
graphs.alt: Near point in centimeters against age from 10 to 60 years. The curve rises slowly from about 7 cm at 10 years to about 22 cm at 40, then steeply: about 29 cm at 45, 40 cm at 50, 57 cm at 55 and 100 cm at 60. A horizontal line marks a typical reading distance of 35 cm.

questions.q: Read the average near point at age 50.
questions.why: About 40 cm, farther than a comfortable reading distance, so a 50-year-old holds small print at arm’s length. At 20 it was only about 10 cm.

questions.q: At about what age does the average near point pass a typical reading distance of 35 cm?
options: About 45 to 50
About 20 to 25
About 30 to 35
Not until after 60

why.correct: The curve crosses the 35 cm line between 45 and 50, which is when most people first need reading glasses.
options: Right: the mid-40s to 50.
At 20 to 25 the near point is only about 10 to 12 cm.
At 30 to 35 it is still under 20 cm.
By 60 it is about a meter, far past reading distance.

questions.q: From 40 on, the same eyes are tested wearing convex reading glasses. How does the curve with the glasses compare?
options: It is lower: they can focus closer at every age
It is higher: the near point moves farther away
It is unchanged: glasses cannot change the near point
It becomes a flat line at 35 cm

why.correct: A convex lens adds the bending the stiff lens can no longer add, so near objects come to a focus again, and the near point moves closer. The glasses do nothing for the lens itself, which keeps stiffening.
options: Right: added bending, closer focus.
A convex lens adds bending; that brings the near point closer, not farther.
The near point depends on the total bending available, and the glasses add to it.
The glasses add a fixed amount of bending, so the curve still rises with age, just lower.

graphs.title: Hearing thresholds across frequencies (an audiogram)
graphs.intro: Each line shows the quietest tone one ear can hear at each frequency, in decibels hearing level (dB HL), where 0 is what an average healthy young ear can just hear. As on a clinical audiogram, lower on the graph means a louder tone was needed: worse hearing.
graphs.alt: Hearing threshold in dB HL against frequency, at 250, 500, 1,000, 2,000, 4,000 and 8,000 Hz, drawn as on a clinical audiogram: 0 dB HL near the top, and lines sit lower where hearing is worse. A healthy young ear stays near the top, between 5 and 10 dB HL. A noise-damaged ear is near normal at low frequencies but dips down to about 55 dB HL at 4,000 Hz and comes back up to 30 at 8,000 Hz. A typical 70-year-old ear slopes steadily down from 15 dB HL at 250 Hz to 60 at 8,000 Hz. A line at 25 dB HL marks the limit of normal hearing.

questions.q: Read the noise-damaged ear’s threshold at 4,000 Hz.
questions.why: About 55 dB HL: a 4,000 Hz tone must be about 55 dB louder than the average healthy young ear needs (0 dB HL). On the logarithmic decibel scale that is several hundred thousand times the sound intensity.

questions.q: Where does the noise-damaged ear show its typical dip (notch)?
options: Around 4,000 Hz
At 250 Hz, the lowest tone tested
Evenly across every frequency
Only at 8,000 Hz, the highest tone tested

why.correct: Years of loud noise destroy hair cells, especially outer hair cells, in the part of the cochlea tuned near 4,000 Hz, close to the base. That notch in the consonant range makes speech sound muffled.
options: Right: a notch near 4,000 Hz.
Low frequencies are tuned near the apex, and they are close to normal in this ear.

An even loss across frequencies is not the noise pattern. It can come from a conductive block such as fluid in the middle ear, but only bone-conduction testing tells conductive from sensorineural loss.
The line is worst at 4,000 Hz and partly recovers at 8,000 Hz. A steady fall toward 8,000 Hz is the pattern of aging.

questions.q: Which frequencies does the 70-year-old ear hear worst?
options: The highest, 4,000 to 8,000 Hz
The lowest, 250 to 500 Hz
The middle, 1,000 to 2,000 Hz
All frequencies equally

why.correct: Age-related loss usually starts at the highest frequencies, which are detected at the base of the cochlea, and spreads downward.
options: Right: high frequencies first.
The low tones are the best-preserved part of this line.
The middle tones are affected, but less than the high ones.
The line slopes steadily down toward the high frequencies; it is not flat.

questions.q: Fluid fills the middle ear of the healthy young ear, blocking about 30 dB of sound at every frequency. How does its line change?
options: It moves down evenly at every frequency
It dips only at 4,000 Hz
It moves up, above the 0 dB HL line
It does not change, because the cochlea is healthy

why.correct: Fluid damps the eardrum and ossicles, so less sound of any pitch reaches the oval window. The whole air-conduction line moves down: a conductive loss. Tested by bone conduction, the same ear would still be normal.
options: Right: an even, conductive loss.
A notch at 4,000 Hz comes from damaged hair cells in one part of the cochlea, not from a middle ear block.
Above the 0 line would mean better than average hearing; fluid makes hearing worse.
Air conduction depends on the middle ear too. The healthy cochlea shows up only when sound bypasses the middle ear through the bone.

graphs.title: Heart rate as each division is blocked
graphs.intro: Two resting volunteers each receive two drugs, 8 minutes apart: atropine, which blocks vagal ACh at muscarinic receptor proteins, and a beta blocker, which blocks sympathetic NE and epinephrine at beta receptor proteins. One gets atropine first; the other gets the beta blocker first.
graphs.alt: Heart rate in beats per minute against time from 0 to 20 minutes. Both start at 70. The atropine-first line climbs after the first drug at 2 minutes to about 108, then falls to about 100 after the beta blocker at 10 minutes. The beta-blocker-first line dips to about 62 after the first drug, then climbs to about 100 after atropine. Both end at about 100, the heart’s own rate.

questions.q: With both drugs working (after about 13 minutes), read the heart rate.
questions.why: About 100 beats a minute on both lines. With both divisions blocked, the heart beats at its own intrinsic rate, the rate a transplanted heart without nerves shows.

questions.q: By how many beats a minute did atropine alone raise the rate, from 70 to its plateau?
questions.why: From 70 to about 108, a rise of about 38. Removing vagal tone changes the resting rate far more than removing sympathetic tone, because at rest vagal tone dominates the heart.

questions.q: Which part of the record shows the heart with only its sympathetic tone removed, and vagal tone still working?
options: Minutes 4 to 10 on the beta-blocker-first line
Minutes 4 to 10 on the atropine-first line
After minute 13, once both drugs are working, on both lines
The first 2 minutes on both lines

why.correct: The beta blocker has removed the sympathetic push, and vagal tone, unopposed, holds the rate at about 62, just below the resting 70.
options: Right: sympathetic blocked, vagus working.
On the atropine-first line those minutes show vagal tone removed and sympathetic tone still working, so the rate is higher.
After minute 13 both divisions are blocked.
In the first 2 minutes both divisions are working: the normal resting state.

questions.q: The atropine-first test is repeated in a heart transplant recipient, whose cardiac nerves are cut. How does the line change?
options: It starts near 100 and barely moves
It rises even higher after atropine
It starts at 70 and rises to 108 as before
It falls to 40 after the beta blocker

why.correct: With no nerves there is no vagal tone to hold the rate down, so it starts near the intrinsic 100, and atropine has nothing to block. The beta blocker lowers it only slightly, by blocking the small effect of circulating epinephrine.
options: Right: already at its own rate.
Atropine can only raise the rate by removing vagal tone, and a transplanted heart has none.
A resting rate of 70 depends on vagal tone, which needs the cut vagus nerve.
The beta blocker can only remove the small push from circulating epinephrine, a few beats a minute. With no vagal tone, nothing can pull the rate far down.

graphs.title: Reading a hematocrit tube
graphs.intro: Four blood samples were spun in a centrifuge. In each tube the blood fills 80 mm: packed red cells at the bottom, a buffy coat too thin to measure, and plasma above. Hematocrit = height of the red column ÷ height of the whole blood column × 100%.
graphs.alt: Four spun blood tubes side by side, each with blood filling 80 millimeters. The red cell column is 36 mm tall in tube 1, 20 mm in tube 2, 52 mm in tube 3 and 36 mm in tube 4. Plasma fills the rest of each column up to 80 mm.

questions.q: Read the red column in tube 1 and work out its hematocrit.
questions.why: The red column is 36 mm and the blood column is 80 mm. 36 ÷ 80 = 0.45, so the hematocrit is 45%, within the usual range for either sex. The other 55% is plasma, plus a buffy coat of well under 1%.

questions.q: Work out the hematocrit of tube 3.
questions.why: The red column is 52 mm of an 80 mm blood column: 52 ÷ 80 = 0.65, or 65%. That is well above the usual top of about 52% in men, so red cells make up an unusually large share of the blood.

questions.q: Which tube has the lowest share of red cells?
options: Tube 2
Tube 1
Tube 3
Tube 4

why.correct: Tube 2’s red column is 20 mm of 80 mm: a hematocrit of 25%, far below the usual range. Its plasma layer is correspondingly deep.
options: Right: 20 ÷ 80 = 25%, the shortest red column of the four.
Tube 1 is 36 ÷ 80 = 45%, in the usual range.
Tube 3 has the tallest red column, 65%.
Tube 4 is 36 ÷ 80 = 45%, the same share as tube 1.

questions.q: Tube 1 is last week’s sample from a man who is healthy. Tube 4 is his sample drawn two minutes after he lost about a liter of blood from a deep cut. What does tube 4 show?
options: Nothing yet: cells and plasma were lost together, so the share is unchanged
A lab error, because a large bleed must lower the hematocrit at once
That he has more red cells than last week
That his plasma was lost but not his red cells

why.correct: A hematocrit is a ratio, not an amount. Whole blood leaves the body with cells and plasma in their usual proportion, so right after the bleed the share is unchanged. It falls over the following hours as fluid moves into the blood from the tissues and dilutes the remaining cells.
options: Right: the ratio cannot show a loss of whole blood until fluid moves in and dilutes the cells.
The result is expected. A hematocrit says nothing by itself about how much blood a person has.
The red column is the same share as last week. He has fewer red cells in total, but the ratio hides it.
Losing only plasma would raise the hematocrit, as in dehydration. Tube 4 matches tube 1.

questions.q: The man who gave tube 1 has 5 L of blood. He is given 2 L of salt solution through a drip, which for this question stays in his blood, and a new sample is spun. How does the red column in his tube change?
options: Shorter: about 26 mm, a hematocrit of about 32%
Taller, because the drip adds volume to the blood
Unchanged, because no red cells were added or lost
Shorter: about 10 mm, because the drip destroys red cells

why.correct: His red cell volume is 45% of 5 L = 2.25 L. After the drip, the same 2.25 L sits in 7 L of blood: 2.25 ÷ 7 = 0.32, so the hematocrit is about 32%, and the red column in an 80 mm sample is about 0.32 × 80 = 26 mm. Adding plasma volume lowers the hematocrit without removing a single red cell.
options: Right: the same red cells are spread through more blood.
The added volume is fluid, not cells, so red cells become a smaller share of the sample.
The number of red cells is unchanged, but the hematocrit is a share, and the share falls.
Salt solution matched to the blood does not destroy red cells. The fall comes from dilution alone.

graphs.title: Hematocrit and reticulocytes after a bleed
graphs.intro: A healthy woman loses about 1 L of her 5 L of blood in one sudden bleed and gets no transfusion. The top panel shows her hematocrit over the next eight weeks; the bottom shows her reticulocytes as a percentage of red cells. The numbers are typical, not from one patient.
graphs.alt: Two panels over 56 days after a bleed. Top: hematocrit starts at 45%, falls over the first two to three days to about 36% as fluid moves into the blood, stays near 36% until about day 5, then climbs slowly back to about 45% by day 56. Bottom: reticulocytes stay near 1% for the first two days, rise from day 3 to a peak of about 4% around day 7 to 10, then drift back toward 1% by day 56.

questions.q: Read her hematocrit on day 3.
questions.why: About 36%. She lost a fifth of her red cells: 45% of 5 L is 2.25 L, less 0.45 L lost, leaves 1.8 L. Once fluid from her tissues, and then water she drinks and her kidneys hold back, has refilled her blood to about 5 L, 1.8 ÷ 5 = 36%.

questions.q: Read the highest reticulocyte percentage.
questions.why: About 4%, around a week after the bleed: roughly four times the normal 1%. EPO has sped up her marrow, and the reticulocytes show it.

questions.q: In which period does the hematocrit fall even though she is not losing any more red cells?
options: The first two to three days
Days 3 to 10
Weeks 2 to 8
Only the first minute after the bleed

why.correct: Right after the bleed the hematocrit is unchanged, because cells and plasma were lost together. Over the next two to three days, fluid moves into the blood from the tissues and dilutes the remaining red cells, so the share falls.
options: Right: this fall is dilution, not a new loss of cells.
By then the hematocrit is flat and starting to climb, as the marrow speeds up.
In these weeks the hematocrit rises, as new red cells are added.
In the first minute, cells and plasma leave together, so the hematocrit has not yet changed.

questions.q: When does the marrow’s response first show in her blood?
options: From about day 3, as reticulocytes rise
Within an hour, as the hematocrit falls
Only after four weeks
Never: the marrow cannot respond to a bleed

why.correct: Less oxygen reaching the kidneys raises EPO within hours, but precursors need 3–5 days to mature and release extra reticulocytes. That rise is the first sign in the blood that the marrow has sped up.
options: Right: reticulocytes climb from about day 3.
The early fall in hematocrit is dilution. The marrow cannot add cells that fast.
The reticulocyte count is already near its peak in the first two weeks.
A healthy marrow facing blood loss speeds up; that is why reticulocytes rise in hemorrhagic anemia.

questions.q: The same bleed happens to a woman whose iron stores were already empty. How do her curves differ?
options: The reticulocyte peak is lower and the hematocrit recovers more slowly
The reticulocyte peak is higher, because EPO is higher
The hematocrit does not fall in the first days
The curves are the same, because her marrow and kidneys are healthy

why.correct: Her kidneys sense the low oxygen and EPO rises, but her marrow has too little iron to build hemoglobin. It cannot speed up, so the reticulocyte rise is small, the new cells are small and pale, and the hematocrit stays low for much longer. The early dilution is the same.
options: Right: the effector lacks a raw material, so a strong signal gets a weak response.
EPO may be high, but the marrow cannot answer it without iron for heme.
The early fall is dilution by fluid from the tissues, which happens whatever the iron stores.
Healthy marrow and kidneys are not enough: every hemoglobin molecule needs iron.

graphs.title: Blood glucose and insulin after a meal
graphs.intro: Blood glucose and plasma insulin over the three hours after a carbohydrate meal eaten at time 0. The top panel also shows a person with type 2 diabetes. Values are typical, not from one person.
graphs.alt: Two stacked graphs over 180 minutes after a meal. Top: blood glucose in mg/dL. In a healthy person it starts at about 88, peaks at about 134 at 45 minutes, falls below 100 by about 2 hours and dips to about 85 at 2.5 to 3 hours. In type 2 diabetes it starts at 140, peaks at about 240 at 90 minutes and is still about 190 at 3 hours. Bottom: plasma insulin in the healthy person in microunits per mL, starting at about 6, rising within 5 minutes, peaking at about 58 at 45 minutes and falling to about 7 by 3 hours.

questions.q: Read the highest blood glucose the healthy person reaches.
questions.why: About 134 mg/dL, at about 45 minutes. After a meal, glucose in a healthy person usually peaks below 140 mg/dL.

questions.q: Read the peak plasma insulin in the healthy person.
questions.why: About 58 µU/mL, nearly ten times the fasting level of about 6, reached at about 45 minutes, the same time as the glucose peak. Insulin rises and falls with glucose because the beta cells respond to it directly.

questions.q: Read the blood glucose of the person with type 2 diabetes two hours after the meal.
questions.why: About 228 mg/dL. A glucose of 200 mg/dL or more two hours after a standard glucose drink is one of the diagnostic criteria for diabetes. Insulin-resistant muscle, fat and liver clear the glucose slowly.

questions.q: During which stretch is insulin falling while glucose returns toward its fasting level?
options: About 45 to 120 minutes
The first 45 minutes
After about 140 minutes, when glucose is lowest
Throughout the three hours

why.correct: After the 45-minute peak, insulin is moving glucose into muscle, fat and liver, so glucose falls. As it falls, beta cell ATP falls, potassium channels reopen and insulin release drops: the response removes its own stimulus.
options: Right: both fall together from about 45 to 120 minutes.
In the first 45 minutes both glucose and insulin are rising.
By then glucose has already returned and slightly undershot; insulin is already low.
Insulin rises for the first 45 minutes, then falls.

questions.q: Where does the healthy person’s glucose dip slightly below its starting value, and why?
options: After about 140 minutes: insulin’s effect outlasts the stimulus briefly
At the 45-minute peak, when insulin is at its very highest level
In the first 5 minutes: the meal has not been absorbed
Around 90 minutes: glucagon is released

why.correct: Insulin moved glucose into storage and is still falling back when glucose reaches its starting level, so glucose undershoots a little, to about 85 mg/dL, before glucagon and the liver bring it back.
options: Right: a small undershoot as insulin’s action lags behind glucose.
At 45 minutes glucose is at its highest, not its lowest.
Glucose begins rising within minutes of eating; it does not dip first.
At 90 minutes glucose is still above its starting value, and glucagon raises glucose rather than lowering it.

questions.q: Someone with untreated type 1 diabetes eats the same meal. How does the insulin curve change?
options: It stays flat near zero
It rises higher than normal to make up for the glucose
It peaks later but reaches the same height
It is unchanged; only the glucose curve differs

why.correct: In type 1 diabetes the immune system has destroyed the beta cells, so almost no insulin is released, however high glucose climbs. With nothing to move glucose into muscle and fat, glucose would rise even higher than in type 2.
options: Right: no beta cells, no insulin response.
That is what beta cells do in early type 2 diabetes. In type 1 they are gone.
A late but normal peak would need working beta cells.
The insulin curve is exactly what fails in type 1 diabetes.

questions.q: In early type 2 diabetes, muscle, fat and liver respond weakly to insulin, but the beta cells still work well. Blood glucose after the meal is near normal. How does the insulin curve compare with the healthy one?
options: Higher and longer-lasting
Lower
Flat near zero
The same, because glucose is the same

why.correct: Each unit of insulin does less, so glucose stays a little higher for a little longer and keeps driving the beta cells. They release much more insulin, which keeps glucose near normal. Only when they can no longer keep up does glucose rise.
options: Right: more insulin makes up for the resistance, for years.
Lower insulin would let glucose climb; that happens only late, when the beta cells fail.
A flat curve means no beta cells, as in type 1 diabetes.
The same glucose is being held only because more insulin is needed to hold it.

graphs.title: Primary and secondary antibody responses
graphs.intro: Antibody against one antigen in the serum of a person exposed to it at day 0 and again at day 50. IgM and IgG are drawn separately. The gap between exposures is shortened to fit the page; memory lasts years. Values are typical, not from one person.
graphs.alt: Antibody level in relative units over 80 days. After the first exposure at day 0 nothing appears for about 5 days. IgM rises from about day 6 to a small peak of about 6 at day 10 and falls away by day 30. IgG rises from about day 8 to a peak of about 8 at day 14 and falls to about 1 by day 50. After the second exposure at day 50, IgG starts rising within 1 to 2 days, climbs steeply to about 100 by day 59 and is still about 75 at day 80. IgM makes only a small bump of about 3 after the second exposure.

questions.q: On about which day after the first exposure does IgG reach its primary peak?
questions.why: About day 14. The few naïve B cells that fit had to be selected, expand into clones and become plasma cells, so a primary response peaks one to two weeks after exposure.

questions.q: Read the peak IgG level after the second exposure.
questions.why: About 100 relative units, reached about 9 days after the second exposure. Memory B cells far outnumber the original naïve cells and produce many more plasma cells.

questions.q: About how many times higher is the secondary IgG peak than the primary IgG peak?
questions.why: About 100 ÷ 8 ≈ 12 times. Secondary peaks are often 10 to 100 times higher than primary ones; this graph sits at the low end of that range.

questions.q: Where is the lag of the primary response, when the antigen is present but no antibody has appeared yet?
options: Days 0 to about 6
Days 6 to 14
Days 50 to 52
Days 60 to 80

why.correct: For about the first 5 days nothing is measurable. The rare naïve B cells that fit are being selected, helped by helper T cells and expanded, and antibody appears only once plasma cells form.
options: Right: no antibody is detectable for the first 5 or so days.
By then antibody is rising; this is the primary response itself, first IgM, then IgG.
That is the much shorter lag of the secondary response, only 1 to 2 days here.
This is the secondary response staying high, not a lag.

questions.q: During which stretch is IgM the main antibody class?
options: About days 6 to 11
About days 14 to 30
About days 52 to 60
Throughout both responses

why.correct: Every B cell starts out making IgM. Class switching to IgG takes a few more days, so IgM leads early in the primary response. Finding IgM against a microbe therefore points to a current or recent infection.
options: Right: IgM rises and peaks first, then IgG overtakes it.
By then IgG has overtaken IgM, and IgM is falling away.
Memory B cells have already switched class, so the secondary response is mostly IgG.
IgM leads only early in the first response; after that IgG dominates.

questions.q: Suppose that at day 50 the person meets a different antigen, one never met before, instead of the same one again. What does IgG against the new antigen do?
options: A slow, small rise like the first response
The same fast, steep rise as the secondary response
A fast rise to a level halfway between the two peaks
No rise at all, because the immune system is still busy

why.correct: Memory is specific. The memory B cells from the first exposure fit only the first antigen, so a new antigen must start from the few naïve cells that fit it: a lag of about a week and a low peak.
options: Right: a new antigen gets a primary response, whatever else the body has met.
A fast, steep rise needs memory cells for that very antigen, and none exist yet.
Memory for one antigen gives no partial head start against another.
Many different clones respond at once; meeting one antigen does not stop a response to another.

questions.q: A one-year-old gets two doses of a vaccine made only of a bacterial capsule sugar, a T cell-independent antigen, at day 0 and day 50. How does the response to the second dose compare with the graph?
options: Mostly IgM and small, with little boost from the first dose
Larger and faster than the secondary response shown
The same as the secondary response shown
Mostly IgE, because sugars switch B cells to IgE

why.correct: Repeating sugar chains cross-link many B cell receptor proteins and switch B cells on without helper T cells. Without that help there is little class switching, little improvement of fit and few memory cells, and children under about 2 respond poorly anyway. That is why capsule sugars are attached to a protein in conjugate vaccines.
options: Right: without helper T cell help, the second dose looks much like the first.
A bigger, faster response needs memory B cells, which T cell-independent antigens barely make.
The response on the graph depends on helper T cells, which a sugar alone does not recruit.
Switching to IgE needs helper T cell contact and IL-4; sugars alone give mostly IgM.

graphs.title: The course of untreated HIV infection
graphs.intro: CD4 count and HIV in the blood over the years of an untreated infection. The first weeks are stretched out on the left; the rest of the axis is in years. The curves are schematic: timing varies widely between people.
graphs.alt: Two stacked graphs. The time axis runs from infection through 2 weeks, 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, then 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 11 years. Top: CD4 count falls from about 1,000 per microliter to about 600 at 3 to 4 weeks, as the virus peaks, recovers partway to about 800 by 6 months, then falls steadily to about 520 at 5 years and crosses 200 at about 10 years. Bottom: HIV in the blood, on a log scale, soars to about 10 million copies per mL at 3 to 4 weeks, falls to a steady level of about 30,000 by 6 months, then slowly climbs again in later years.

questions.q: Read the CD4 count five years after infection.
questions.why: About 520 per microliter, within or just below the normal range of about 500 to 1,500. Most people feel well at this stage, although the count is falling year after year.

questions.q: Read the peak of HIV in the blood during the acute phase, in log10 copies per mL.
questions.why: About 7, which is 10 to the 7th: about 10 million copies per mL. In the first weeks nothing specific is acting against the virus yet, so it multiplies explosively and the person is highly infectious.

questions.q: During which stretch can an antibody test be negative even though the person is infected and highly infectious?
options: The first weeks to 3 months
Between 1 and 5 years
After the CD4 count falls below 200
At no point: the test is always positive once infected

why.correct: This is the window period before seroconversion. A primary antibody response takes time, so antibody usually becomes detectable within a few weeks to 3 months, while virus in the blood is at its highest.
options: Right: before seroconversion the antibody test can miss the infection.
By then antibody has long been present; the test is positive.
Antibody is still present in AIDS; the test stays positive.
Antibody takes weeks to appear, so an early test can be falsely negative.

questions.q: Where is the virus held at a lower, steady level, and what mainly holds it there?
options: The chronic phase; cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells
The chronic phase; antibodies neutralize the free virus
The acute phase; helper T cells kill the virus directly
The AIDS stretch; the virus runs out of cells to infect

why.correct: CD8 cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells before they release new virus, bringing the level down after the acute peak and holding it for years. They never clear it, because silent virus hides in some memory T cells.
options: Right: the fall and the steady level come mainly from cytotoxic T cells.
Antibodies appear, but the error-prone virus mutates around them; they are not what controls it.
Helper T cells kill nothing themselves, and in the acute phase the virus is rising, not held steady.
In AIDS the virus rises again as cytotoxic responses fail without helper T cells.

questions.q: Combination antiretroviral therapy is started five years after infection. How do the two curves change?
options: HIV falls below detection and the CD4 count climbs
HIV falls below detection, but the CD4 count keeps falling
The CD4 count climbs, but HIV in the blood is unchanged
Both curves stay the same; the drugs act only on latent virus

why.correct: The drugs block viral enzymes, so new cells stop being infected and HIV in the blood falls below detection. With fewer helper T cells being killed, the CD4 count recovers. The drugs cannot reach silent DNA inside memory T cells, so they control HIV without curing it.
options: Right: virus falls and helper T cells recover.
With the virus suppressed, helper T cells are no longer being destroyed, so the count recovers.
The CD4 count rises because the virus falls: fewer helper T cells are being killed, so one change drives the other.
The drugs block viral enzymes in active infection; latent virus is exactly what they cannot reach.

graphs.title: Stomach pH and gastrin around a meal
graphs.intro: The pH of the stomach contents and the gastrin level in the blood, from half an hour before a protein-rich meal eaten at time 0 until four hours after it. The curves are schematic, drawn from typical values.
graphs.alt: Two stacked graphs over time from 30 minutes before a meal to 240 minutes after. Top: pH of the stomach contents. It sits near 2 before the meal, jumps to about 5 within minutes of eating, stays near 5 for about 30 minutes, then falls, crossing 3 at about 90 minutes and reaching about 1.6 by 4 hours. Bottom: gastrin in the blood, near 20 pg/mL before the meal, rising to a peak of about 85 at 40 minutes, then falling back to about 20 by 4 hours as the pH drops below 3.

questions.q: Read the pH of the stomach contents 15 minutes after the meal.
questions.why: About 5. Food, especially protein, buffers the acid already in the stomach, so the pH jumps from about 2 to about 5 even though acid secretion is rising.

questions.q: Read the peak gastrin level, in pg/mL.
questions.why: About 85 pg/mL, four times the fasting level, 40 minutes into the meal. Protein fragments, stretch and vagal signals all drive the G cells while the pH is still high.

questions.q: Where does food buffering the acid help gastrin rise?
options: The first hour or so after eating
The half hour before the meal
From 90 minutes on
Only at the very end, after 3 hours

why.correct: While food holds the pH above 3, D cells release little somatostatin, so nothing brakes the G cells. Protein, stretch and vagal signals push gastrin up.
options: Right: a high pH means no somatostatin brake while the G cells are being stimulated.
Before the meal the pH is near 2 and there is no protein to stimulate the G cells, so gastrin stays low.
By then the pH has fallen below 3 and gastrin is falling, not rising.
Late in the meal the pH is lowest and gastrin is back near its fasting level.

questions.q: Where is gastrin falling because the acid itself is switching it off?
options: From about 90 minutes on, once the pH is below 3
In the first 20 minutes after eating
Before the meal
Nowhere: gastrin falls only when the meal leaves the stomach

why.correct: As acid accumulates, the pH in the antrum drops below about 3, D cells release somatostatin, and the G cells slow down: the product switches off its own stimulus.
options: Right: low pH, somatostatin, less gastrin. Negative feedback.
Gastrin is climbing steeply in the first 20 minutes, while the pH is high.
Before the meal gastrin is low and flat, not falling.
Gastrin falls while food is still in the stomach, because the pH has dropped; that is the feedback loop at work.

questions.q: The same person eats the same meal after a week of taking a proton pump inhibitor. How do the two curves change?
options: pH stays high and gastrin stays higher for longer
pH falls lower and gastrin falls lower
pH is unchanged, but gastrin rises higher
Neither changes, because the drug acts only between meals

why.correct: The drug blocks the proton pumps, so little acid is made and the pH never falls below 3. Without low pH there is little somatostatin, so the brake on the G cells stays off and gastrin runs higher and longer. The parietal cells cannot answer it, because their pumps are blocked.
options: Right: no acid, no brake, more gastrin.
Less acid means a higher pH, not a lower one, and a higher pH removes the brake on gastrin.
Blocking the pumps is exactly what changes the pH: less H+ reaches the stomach contents.
Omeprazole blocks pumps that are working after a meal as well; that is when it matters most.

graphs.title: How fast the stomach empties
graphs.intro: The share of a drink of water and of a mixed solid meal still in the stomach over the four hours after swallowing, as measured by imaging. The curves are schematic, drawn from typical values for healthy adults.
graphs.alt: A graph of percent of the meal remaining in the stomach, from 100 at time 0 down to 0, over 240 minutes. Water empties at once and fast: about 42% remains at 20 minutes, 8% at 1 hour and none by 2 hours. The mixed solid meal barely leaves for the first 30 minutes, then empties steadily: about 72% remains at 1 hour, 36% at 2 hours and 5% at 4 hours. A dashed line marks 50%.

questions.q: About how many minutes does it take for half of the water to leave the stomach?
questions.why: About 15 to 20 minutes. Liquid needs no grinding, so it starts passing the pylorus within minutes.

questions.q: What percent of the mixed meal is still in the stomach 2 hours after eating?
questions.why: About a third. A mixed meal takes 2 to 4 hours to leave, a few milliliters at a time.

questions.q: For the first half hour the solid meal hardly leaves, though water empties at once. What is the stomach doing in that stretch?
options: Grinding the solids into particles small enough to pass the pylorus
Waiting for the small intestine to release gastrin
Absorbing the nutrients before passing them on
Holding the pylorus wide open while acid builds up in the stomach contents

why.correct: Mixing waves drive the contents against a closing pylorus. Only the most liquid part squirts through; solid pieces are flung back and ground until they are smaller than about 1 to 2 mm. Until enough chyme is made, little solid leaves.
options: Right: solids must become chyme before they can pass.
Gastrin comes from the stomach’s own G cells and mainly drives acid; it is not what holds solids back.
The stomach absorbs almost no nutrients; alcohol and aspirin are among the few things that cross its lining.
The pylorus closes as each wave arrives; that is what holds the solids back for grinding.

questions.q: The same meal is eaten with a large amount of added fat. How does the solid-meal curve change?
options: It empties more slowly: the curve lies higher
It empties faster: the curve lies lower
It is unchanged; fat affects only digestion, not emptying
The lag disappears, and it empties as fast as water

why.correct: Fat reaching the first part of the small intestine releases CCK and triggers the enterogastric reflex. They weaken the antrum’s waves and tighten the pylorus, so fat empties slowest of all the nutrients.
options: Right: fat releases the most CCK, and CCK slows emptying.
Fat does the opposite: it holds food in the stomach longer.
The pace of emptying is set by what the small intestine receives, and fat is its strongest brake.
Solids still need grinding, and fat adds a brake; nothing about fat makes a meal behave like water.

questions.q: Years of diabetes have damaged a man’s vagus nerves and enteric neurons. How does his solid-meal curve compare?
options: Far slower: much of the meal is still there at 4 hours
Faster, because the pylorus no longer closes
The same, because the pacesetter cells still make slow waves
Faster for water, and unchanged for solids

why.correct: Slow waves set the rhythm, but nerves decide whether each wave produces a contraction. With the nerves damaged, the mixing waves are weak, solids are ground slowly and the stomach empties very slowly: gastroparesis. Food is vomited undigested hours later.
options: Right: weak waves, slow grinding, slow emptying.
The problem is weak contraction of the antrum, which slows emptying rather than speeding it.
A slow wave alone rarely makes the muscle contract; without the nerves, most waves produce no contraction.
Liquids empty more slowly too, though less dramatically; the solid curve is the one most affected.

graphs.title: The hydrogen breath test for low lactase
graphs.intro: Hydrogen in exhaled breath after drinking 50 g of lactose at time 0, in a person who still makes lactase and in one who does not. A rise of 20 parts per million or more above the starting level is the usual cutoff for poor lactose digestion. The curves are schematic, drawn from typical values.
graphs.alt: A graph of hydrogen in the breath, in parts per million, over 180 minutes after drinking lactose. The person who makes lactase stays near 5 to 7 the whole time. The person with low lactase stays near 5 to 10 for the first hour, then rises, crossing 25 at about 90 minutes and reaching about 62 at 3 hours. A dashed line at 25 marks 20 above the starting level.

questions.q: Read the breath hydrogen of the person with low lactase at 150 minutes.
questions.why: About 58 ppm, more than 50 above the starting level. Colon bacteria are fermenting the undigested lactose, and some of their hydrogen is breathed out.

questions.q: At about what time does the low-lactase curve cross the cutoff line?
questions.why: At about 90 minutes. The test is positive from then on, because hydrogen has risen more than 20 ppm above where it started.

questions.q: Why is there almost no rise in the first hour, even in the person with low lactase?
options: The lactose has not yet reached the colon
SGLT1 is absorbing the lactose in that hour
Stomach acid digests the lactose first
Lactase works only in the first hour

why.correct: The hydrogen comes from bacteria fermenting lactose in the colon. It takes time for the drink to leave the stomach and pass along the small intestine, so the rise starts only when the undigested lactose arrives.
options: Right: no lactose in the colon yet, so no fermentation.
SGLT1 carries glucose and galactose, not lactose. Lactose must first be split by lactase.
Acid does not split lactose; only lactase at the brush border does.
The person who makes lactase keeps making it; the flat start is about travel time, not enzyme timing.

questions.q: The person with low lactase repeats the test, this time taking lactase tablets with the drink. How does her curve change?
options: It stays near its starting level
It rises earlier and higher
It rises just as before, because the tablets act only in the colon
It falls below zero

why.correct: The tablets supply the missing enzyme, so most of the lactose is split into glucose and galactose and absorbed in the small intestine. Little reaches the colon, so bacteria make little hydrogen.
options: Right: lactose is digested and absorbed before the colon.
An earlier, higher rise would need more lactose in the colon, and the tablets reduce it.
Lactase has to act in the small intestine, where the products can be absorbed; that is where the tablets work.
Breath hydrogen cannot fall below zero; at most it returns to the starting level.

questions.q: The same person with low lactase takes the test a few days after a course of broad-spectrum antibiotics. How might her curve look?
options: Flatter: the test can miss her low lactase
Higher, because antibiotics destroy lactase
Unchanged, because the hydrogen comes from her own cells
Earlier, because antibiotics speed up the gut

why.correct: The hydrogen is made by colon bacteria, not by her cells. With many bacteria killed, the undigested lactose is fermented less, the rise may stay below the cutoff, and the test gives a false negative. She may still get diarrhea from the lactose’s osmotic effect.
options: Right: fewer bacteria, less hydrogen, a falsely reassuring result.
Antibiotics kill bacteria; they do not act on lactase in her own cells.
Human cells do not make hydrogen gas. Only the bacteria’s fermentation does.
Timing depends on how fast the lactose reaches the colon; the main change is how much hydrogen is made there.

graphs.title: GFR and arterial pressure: the autoregulation plateau
graphs.intro: Glomerular filtration rate of both kidneys against mean arterial pressure, with the kidney’s own controls working (solid) and, for comparison, if GFR simply followed pressure (dashed). The curves are schematic, drawn from typical values in the chapter’s figure.
graphs.alt: A graph of GFR in mL/min, 0 to 150, against mean arterial pressure in mm Hg, 0 to 200. The solid curve with autoregulation is zero at 40 mm Hg, climbs steeply to about 55 at 60 and 117 at 80, stays almost flat between 80 and 180 (about 123 at 100 and 132 at 180), then climbs again above 180. The dashed line without autoregulation rises straight from zero at 40 mm Hg through 125 at 100 mm Hg to 150 at about 112 mm Hg.

questions.q: Read the GFR at a normal mean arterial pressure of 100 mm Hg.
questions.why: About 120 to 125 mL/min, the normal GFR of a young adult: about 180 liters of filtrate a day.

questions.q: After a large bleed, mean arterial pressure falls to 60 mm Hg. Read the GFR.
questions.why: About 55 mL/min, less than half of normal. At 60 mm Hg the pressure is below the plateau, so the afferent arterioles are already as wide as they can go and GFR falls with pressure.

questions.q: Suppose GFR simply followed pressure. Read the GFR on the dashed line at a MAP of 110 mm Hg, as when you are startled.
questions.why: About 145 mL/min, some 20 mL/min more than normal. Fluid would rush through the tubules faster than they could reabsorb it, and salt, water and nutrients would be lost. The solid curve at 110 barely moves.

questions.q: Over which range of mean arterial pressure does GFR barely change?
options: About 80 to 180 mm Hg
About 0 to 40 mm Hg
About 40 to 80 mm Hg
Only above about 180 mm Hg, where the arterioles are fully narrowed

why.correct: Between about 80 and 180 mm Hg, the myogenic mechanism and tubuloglomerular feedback adjust the afferent arterioles so GBHP, and so GFR, stay nearly constant. Some courses quote 60 to 150 mm Hg, a round figure for organs in general; the kidney’s own plateau starts a little higher and goes further.
options: Right: the plateau of the solid curve.
Below about 40 mm Hg, GBHP is too low to overcome CHP and BCOP, and filtration stops.
Here the curve climbs steeply: autoregulation cannot keep up, and GFR falls with pressure.
Above 180 mm Hg the afferent arterioles cannot narrow any further, so GFR rises again.

questions.q: A man in shock has a MAP of 65 mm Hg, and his urine output has dropped. On which part of the curve is he?
options: Below the plateau, where GFR falls with pressure
On the plateau, where the afferent arterioles still hold GFR steady
Above the range, where GFR rises with pressure
Where filtration has stopped completely

why.correct: At 65 mm Hg he is below the plateau. His afferent arterioles cannot widen any further to protect GBHP, so GFR falls steeply, and strong sympathetic activity lowers it still more.
options: Right: below about 80 mm Hg, GFR follows pressure.
The plateau starts at about 80 mm Hg; 65 is below it.
That region is above 180 mm Hg.
Filtration stops only near 40 mm Hg on this curve; at 65 some filtrate is still made.

questions.q: An experimental drug stops both the myogenic mechanism and tubuloglomerular feedback, so the afferent arterioles no longer change their width. How does the GFR curve change?
options: It follows the dashed line: GFR rises and falls with pressure
It stays flat, because the filtration coefficient Kf has not changed at all
It shifts down but stays flat
It shifts to the right but keeps its plateau

why.correct: The plateau exists only because the afferent arteriole narrows as pressure rises and widens as it falls. Without those two mechanisms, GBHP follows arterial pressure, and GFR does too.
options: Right: no autoregulation, no plateau.
Kf sets how much fluid crosses per mm Hg; it cannot hold GFR steady when pressure changes.
A lower flat curve would still need something to hold GFR steady.
Both mechanisms act through the same arteriole; blocking both removes the plateau rather than moving it.

questions.q: During a hemorrhage, strong sympathetic activity constricts the afferent arterioles. How does the GFR curve compare with the solid one?
options: It lies lower: at any pressure, GFR is less
It lies higher: at any pressure, GFR is more
It is unchanged, because autoregulation cancels the nerves
It becomes the dashed line

why.correct: Nervous and hormonal controls can override autoregulation. Strong sympathetic constriction of the afferent arterioles lowers GBHP at every arterial pressure, so less filtrate and less urine are made, saving blood volume.
options: Right: the nerves pull GFR below the plateau.
Sympathetic constriction of the afferent arterioles lowers, not raises, glomerular pressure.
Autoregulation holds GFR steady against changes in pressure; strong sympathetic activity overrides it.
The dashed line shows the loss of autoregulation, not a deliberate lowering by the nerves.

graphs.title: Glucose reabsorption and the transport maximum
graphs.intro: How much glucose both kidneys filter, reabsorb and excrete each minute as plasma glucose rises, at a GFR of 125 mL/min. Drawn from the chapter’s figure; the curves are schematic.
graphs.alt: A graph of glucose in mg/min, 0 to 1,000, against plasma glucose in mg/dL, 0 to 800. The filtered load rises in a straight line from 0 to 1,000 mg/min. The reabsorbed curve follows it up to about 180 mg/dL, bends over and levels off at about 375 mg/min from about 380 mg/dL. The excreted curve is zero up to about 180 mg/dL, then rises, reaching 250 mg/min at 500 mg/dL and running parallel to the filtered line after reabsorption has leveled off.

questions.q: Read the highest rate at which the kidneys can reabsorb glucose.
questions.why: About 375 mg/min, the transport maximum. Every symporter is busy, so more glucose in the filtrate cannot speed reabsorption.

questions.q: At what plasma glucose does glucose first appear in the urine?
questions.why: About 180 mg/dL, the renal threshold, where the excreted curve first rises above zero.

questions.q: Read the filtered load of glucose at a plasma glucose of 100 mg/dL.
questions.why: About 125 mg/min: GFR × plasma glucose = 125 mL/min × 1 mg/mL. It is well below the transport maximum, so all of it is reabsorbed.

questions.q: Plasma glucose is 500 mg/dL. Read how much glucose is excreted each minute.
questions.why: About 250 mg/min: 625 filtered − 375 reabsorbed. Past saturation, every extra milligram filtered is excreted, so the excreted line runs parallel to the filtered one.

questions.q: The renal threshold, 180 mg/dL, is lower than transport maximum ÷ GFR, which would give 300 mg/dL. Which part of the graph shows why?
options: The curved splay between about 180 and 380 mg/dL
The straight filtered line
The flat part of the reabsorbed curve above 380 mg/dL
The region below 180 mg/dL where nothing is excreted

why.correct: Nephrons differ. Some have few carriers for the glucose they filter and saturate early, so glucose starts leaking through them while others still have spare carriers. The bend in the reabsorbed curve and the gradual rise of the excreted curve are that early leak.
options: Right: the splay shows nephrons saturating at different glucose levels.
The filtered load is a straight line; it has nothing to say about carriers.
Above 380 mg/dL every nephron is saturated; the splay comes before that.
Below the threshold every nephron reabsorbs all its glucose, so nothing distinguishes them.

questions.q: In which region does raising plasma glucose further add nothing to the amount reabsorbed?
options: Above about 380 mg/dL
Below about 180 mg/dL
Between 180 and 380 mg/dL
Nowhere: reabsorption always rises with glucose

why.correct: Above about 380 mg/dL every symporter in every nephron is busy: carrier saturation. The reabsorbed curve is flat at the transport maximum.
options: Right: the carriers are saturated.
Below 180 mg/dL reabsorption rises one-for-one with the filtered load.
In the splay, reabsorption is still rising, just more slowly.
A fixed number of carriers sets a ceiling on reabsorption.

questions.q: A drug blocks SGLT2, the symporter that does most of the proximal tubule’s glucose reabsorption. How do the curves change?
options: Reabsorption levels off lower, and glucose spills at normal levels
Reabsorption levels off higher, and the threshold rises
The filtered line becomes steeper
Nothing changes, because the other glucose carriers take over the whole load

why.correct: Fewer working carriers means a lower transport maximum and an earlier start of spillover. Glucose then leaves in the urine even at normal blood levels, which is how the drug lowers blood glucose. The filtered load is unchanged.
options: Right: a lower ceiling and a lower threshold.
Blocking carriers can only lower the ceiling.
The filtered load depends on GFR and plasma glucose, not on the carriers downstream.
The remaining carriers take back only a small share, so the ceiling falls.

graphs.title: Osmolarity along the nephron
graphs.intro: The osmolarity of the fluid inside the tubule at seven points from the start of the proximal tubule to the end of the collecting duct, with high ADH (solid) and no ADH (dashed). Drawn from the chapter’s figure.
graphs.alt: A graph of tubular fluid osmolarity, 0 to 1,300 mOsm/L, at seven points along the nephron. It is 300 at the start and at the end of the proximal tubule, 1,200 at the tip of the loop, about 100 at the start and end of the distal tubule. From there, with high ADH, it rises to 300 at the end of the cortical collecting duct and 1,200 at the end of the collecting duct; with no ADH, it falls to about 75 and then 50. A dotted line marks plasma at 300.

questions.q: Read the osmolarity of the tubular fluid at the tip of a long nephron loop.
questions.why: About 1,200 mOsm/L. The descending limb loses water to the salty inner medulla until its fluid matches it.

questions.q: Read the osmolarity of the fluid entering the distal tubule.
questions.why: About 100 mOsm/L, a third of plasma. The thick ascending limb pumped salt out without letting water follow.

questions.q: With no ADH, read the osmolarity of the urine leaving the collecting duct.
questions.why: About 50 mOsm/L. With no aquaporins, water cannot leave the duct, while it keeps reabsorbing some salt, so the fluid becomes more dilute still.

questions.q: In which segment does the fluid lose about two thirds of its volume but none of its osmolarity?
options: The proximal tubule
The nephron loop
The distal tubule
The collecting duct

why.correct: The proximal tubule reabsorbs solute and water together: water follows solute through aquaporins and leaky tight junctions, so the fluid stays at 300 mOsm/L as its volume falls.
options: Right: flat at 300 across the proximal tubule.
The loop first concentrates the fluid to 1,200 and then dilutes it to 100.
The distal tubule keeps diluting; little water leaves it.
The collecting duct’s osmolarity swings with ADH.

questions.q: Where do the high-ADH and no-ADH paths split?
options: In the collecting duct
In the proximal tubule
At the tip of the loop
In the thick ascending limb

why.correct: ADH acts on principal cells of the late distal tubule and collecting duct. Every segment before them works the same whatever ADH does, so the paths only split there.
options: Right: ADH changes only the last segments.
The proximal tubule reabsorbs water whatever ADH does: obligatory reabsorption.
The loop tip reaches 1,200 either way; the gradient is always there.
The thick ascending limb is nearly waterproof with or without ADH.

questions.q: A patient takes a loop diuretic that blocks NKCC2, and ADH is high. How does the solid curve change?
options: Peak falls, distal fluid less dilute, final urine far below 1,200
The loop peak rises to 2,000
Nothing changes before the collecting duct, because ADH is still high
The proximal tubule fluid falls to 100

why.correct: Without NKCC2 the thick ascending limb stops pumping salt, so it no longer dilutes its fluid and no longer builds the medullary gradient. The descending limb has little salty medulla to lose water to, and even with high ADH the collecting duct can only match a weak gradient. The numbers are schematic.
options: Right: no pumping, no gradient, no concentrated urine.
Blocking the pump can only weaken the gradient.
The drug acts in the loop, so the change starts there.
The proximal tubule is untouched; its fluid stays near 300.

questions.q: Someone on a very low-protein diet makes little urea. With high ADH, how does the end of the solid curve change?
options: The final urine is less concentrated than 1,200
The final urine is more concentrated than 1,200
Only the no-ADH path changes
The proximal tubule fluid falls below 300

why.correct: Urea supplies about half the inner medulla’s osmolarity through urea recycling. With little urea, the inner medulla is less concentrated, so the collecting duct cannot concentrate its fluid as far, even with plenty of ADH. The value shown is schematic.
options: Right: less urea, a weaker inner medulla, less concentrated urine.
Less urea can only weaken the gradient.
The high-ADH path is the one that depends on the inner medulla.
The proximal tubule keeps its fluid at plasma osmolarity.

graphs.title: Urine volume needed to carry the day’s waste
graphs.intro: The daily urine volume needed to excrete 600 mOsm of waste solute, at each possible urine osmolarity: volume = solute ÷ concentration. Your kidneys can make urine from about 50 to 1,200 mOsm/L.
graphs.alt: A curve of daily urine volume in liters, 0 to 12, against urine osmolarity in mOsm/L, 0 to 1,300, for a solute load of 600 mOsm a day. It falls steeply from 12 L at 50 mOsm/L to 6 L at 100 and 2 L at 300, then flattens: 1 L at 600 and 0.5 L at 1,200, the most concentrated urine the kidneys can make.

questions.q: If the kidneys could make urine only at the osmolarity of plasma, 300 mOsm/L, what daily volume would carry 600 mOsm?
questions.why: 600 mOsm ÷ 300 mOsm/L = 2 L. Without the ability to concentrate or dilute, urine volume would be fixed by the solute load.

questions.q: Read the smallest daily urine volume that can carry 600 mOsm.
questions.why: 600 ÷ 1,200 = 0.5 L. No amount of ADH can push urine past the medulla’s 1,200 mOsm/L, so this is the floor.

questions.q: After drinking a lot of water, urine is at 100 mOsm/L. Read the daily volume at that concentration.
questions.why: 600 ÷ 100 = 6 L a day. With ADH low, the kidneys excrete the same solute in far more water.

questions.q: On a hot day without water, where on the curve does your urine sit?
options: Toward the right: concentrated urine, small volume
Toward the left: dilute urine and a large daily volume of it
Exactly at 300 mOsm/L
Below the 0.5 L line

why.correct: High ADH lets water leave the collecting duct into the salty medulla, so urine moves toward 1,200 mOsm/L and the volume toward 0.5 L.
options: Right: concentrated urine, small volume.
That is the low-ADH end, after drinking a lot.
Urine at 300 would mean ADH is doing little either way.
